1.t: First money playing outside bars and in the District
1.s: The boys made two dollars each outside bars, then seven in the District, and his mother was not angry.
1.ch: Becoming a musician: ukulele, clarinet and the Boozaire Kings
1.q: So then we're in business. You dig? Next week's... Now, I know what Ervin(?) Butler ain't givin' us. We got about maybe, say, three-fifths of what we made. He kept that other.

1.t: Leaving the Boozan Kings; playing with old men like Big Eye Louis Nelson
1.s: After two years with the Boozan Kings he played with veterans such as George Glenny, Big Eye Louis Nelson and pianist Wiggins before graduating to Lee Collins.
1.ch: Professional start and leaving New Orleans
1.q: I was 13, 14, 15. It went on about two years. 15 or 16. ’Til I got hip to money to be made in this thing.

1.t: First paid parties with a ukulele, kazoo and washboard band
1.s: With a kazoo player, a fork player and a washboard drummer he played parties for food, drink and then money, which made him a pro.
1.q: Yeah. That’s how I started with the music business. Joe Presser’s son, ’round the corner, who was my good friend, he could blow a kazoo. He was interested in Kid Rena. He knew Kid Rena’s riffs. He knew Buddy Petit’s riffs, Chris Kelly’s riffs. He had that kind of mind. He was destined to become a…

1.t: The stoop band: kazoo, cheese-box drum and Ervin Butler
1.s: Danny drew crowds with ukulele, kazoo and a cheese-box drum, until Ervin Butler offered to take them out to earn money.
1.ch: Becoming a musician: ukulele, clarinet and the Boozaire Kings
1.q: So we're sitting on my steps. Now, Joe Francis Ely(?) is on the corner. He's a presser's son. He gets the kazoo, he comes around. Then with the ukelele, I'm drawing a crowd. I've become a little celebrity with the ukelele.

1.s: Danny organized a band and named it the Boozaire Kings after the Creole word for a good time.
1.ch: Becoming a musician: ukulele, clarinet and the Boozaire Kings
1.q: Now, Herman Henderson was an aristocratic little kid, see. He was there, and... But his people didn't want him hustling or none of that. They had aspired for him to be a little college kid, and his mother was a midwife and his father worked as...he was a helluva mechanic with a big machine company,…

1.t: Teenage spasm band in the District and Decatur Street honky-tonks
1.s: At 16 or 17 Danny led a six-piece spasm band with tin pans, washboard and kazoo and promoted his own gigs.
1.ch: Chicago, Lee Collins and the road
1.q: And there was so much for you to see in this town. You saw a big ocean liner, you'd see all these Oriental people coming in here on those ships. And we began to play in the nightclubs and the little honky-tonks on Decatur Street. When I was 16 and 17, I didn't use(?) any (?)s. We had ...(?)... out…

611.t: Finding work in Boston through brother Herman and Joe Steele
611.s: The first year he worked in restaurants; then his brother Herman's Elks bands spread his name and he began gigging with pianist Joe Steele.
611.q: Well, that's contact, you know. See, for an instance, my brother, he played a little trombone in a amateur Elks' band they called it, see -

611.t: First band at 14 with Charlie Miller
611.s: At 14 he played saxophone in a small swinging combination led by Charlie Miller, playing popular songs.
611.q: Oh. Like the first, well the very first band when I was 14 I was working with a group named Charlie Miller. And we wasn’t playing Dixieland or New Orleans as you may call it, we were swinging. We had a similar Dixieland combination. We had trombone, trumpet, and I was playing saxophone. But…

611.t: Lonnie Polk's band and the Eastern Shore guardian story
611.s: The Polk band played similar jazz around Baltimore, Washington and the Eastern Shore. Waters, underage, needed a guardian trombonist and was caught with sand on his clothes after meeting a girl.
611.q: So that made the band, in some respects made it a little bit, little bit better maybe, could have been. We did a lot of work in Baltimore, in Washington and down in the Eastern shores, see. I never forget that, Eastern shore. I mean, see, I was a - I don't know if I'm allowed to put this on this -

611.t: Soprano and piano duo gigs with Johnny Hodges
611.s: Waters and the younger Johnny Hodges swapped piano and soprano at Saturday tea parties for elite Black college graduates, Hodges getting the gigs as a Boston native.
611.q: Yeah, Johnny - now Johnny and I used to work together. Now here's what we were doing - not at his club, he was working at a club called Black and White Club, he didn't open till 12 o'clock. Now he had to have that same thing that I had, because he

611.t: Reel 2 opening; gigging with Joe Steele in Boston
611.s: After a reel change, Schaap recaps Boston. Waters says the Steele gigs were mostly dancing, that he had no free-solo band, and that money came from commercial jobs.
611.q: No, giggin', yeah. Giggin'. But I did quite a lot with Joe, see, particularly weekends, you know, see.

66.t: The little girl who played for money and with a union band
66.s: As a child she played for teas and neighbours, charging a dollar an hour. At 10 or 12 she played with a union band by ear without reading, and musicians took her out with her mother's trust.
66.q: : that used to dance and we'd make a little money dancing. At one time when I was about 6 or 7 years old I made more money than my stepfather by this. The teachers used to take me home with them and give me a little handkerchief pocket full of money. I'd play for the (musician?), they'd give a…

66.t: The 'little piano girl of East Liberty' and the Pittsburgh parties
66.s: From 6 to 14 she played the parties of wealthy Pittsburgh families, including the Mellons, and her brother-in-law took her to theatres to listen.
66.q: From the age of 6 until I was 14 I was all over the city playing. I played for the Mellons. I became the little piano girl of East Liberty and anytime anybody was having a party or anything they'd say, "Well, let's get the little piano girl." So by this time I was among nothing but the wealthy…

66.t: McKinney's Cotton Pickers take her out on gigs
66.s: When McKinney's Cotton Pickers, including Chu Berry, visited Pittsburgh they picked up the schoolgirl and took her on jobs.
66.q: Yes. When I was in around 5th or 6th grade they used to come to Pittsburgh and they'd drive this big bus on our street, all these musicians, Chu Berry and all of them would take me out on gigs with them.

66.t: Bands in Pittsburgh, the Subway club and Buck and Bubbles
66.s: Visiting bands took her on gigs, and Roland gave her a car. At the Subway on Wiley Avenue she met Buck of Buck and Bubbles, a pianist equal to Waller.
66.ch: Pittsburgh school days and old jealousies
66.q: and nobody knew that. He came to town -

66.t: Running away to play and dating the Seymour and Jeanette stockings
66.s: She ran away to be with musicians until her mother fetched her. She dates the first job with Seymour and Jeanette to about 1925-26 from stockings she still keeps.
66.q: : Well I was still in school, in school for a long time, but see I'd go out in summer vacations. One time I ran away and my mother came and got me.

235.t: High school band's community jobs and pay
235.s: The band played dances and a few clubs for fifty cents up to two dollars.
235.q: High school dances and, after we got popular, we'd do things in the community, you know, like a community dance, you know. When people want to have a dance and then once in a while we'd play a couple of clubs, you know, they'd want us, you know. We were pretty good. Yeah.

235.t: First uniforms: Hartley Toots's band in Cincinnati, 1939
235.s: He first wore band uniforms in Cincinnati at the Cotton Club with Thad and Hank Jones, earning nine dollars a week.
235.ch: Back in New York: Heard and Dizzy
235.q: Well in 1939, durin' the summer vacation from school we went to Cincinnati with Hartley Toots' Band and we met 'em there, Thad Jones and Hank Jones, we were out of...it was the guys from Pontiac and Lansing. There was two from Lansing and...three of us from Lansing, and

235.t: Staying with Sonny Stitt in Saginaw; Jimmy Lucky in Flint
235.s: Working Sunshine Gardens in Saginaw he lodged with the young Sonny Stitt, then went to Flint with Jimmy Lucky's six-piece band.
235.ch: First jobs and finding his sound
235.q: Sunshine Gardens, we done the Sunshine Gardens in Saginaw, but what I'm tryin' to say is that when I was there I stayed in Sonny Stitt 's home. His mother was an ex-chorus girl and he was in high school and when he got out from school he'd come by and we'd practice and I stayed at his house all the…

235.t: How he got the Kelly Martin job: Tweed Beard and his father's request
235.s: After Jimmy Lucky's band, Tweed Beard brought him to Detroit; Kelly Martin hired him and later revealed his father had asked him to.
235.q: Well, what had happened, my father--like I said before--we went to Detroit to visit and we saw Andy Kirk and I first heard Charlie Parker and Jimmy Forrest. But my father, unbeknownst to me, he knew about the Club Congo and I think they were rehearsing that day and we went by there and he got Kelly…

235.t: First gig at Central High, the band books and graduating
235.s: Sy Jenkins and his Orchestra's first dance paid fifty cents; they played Miller, Basie, Lunceford books, he played tenor solos like Marie, and after graduating his father let him try the road instead of college.
235.q: : Oh, Sy Jenkins and his Orchestra. Sure, I remember that. It was at the um...it was a high school dance, Central High School...now it comes to me...Central High School. We played a high

279.t: First vaudeville gig at twelve and the homemade wine
279.s: Uncle takes him to a neighborhood theater to accompany a vaudeville act when the pianist fails to show, and he ends up sick on homemade wine.
279.q: This uncle started easing me in professionally because he gave me a lot of encouragement. And, in fact, when I was about twelve years old he took me to a neighborhood show, a neighborhood theater with him. You know, there was the days when they had silent pictures and they used to have an old piano…

279.t: Hired at the Fern Dance Hall at fourteen
279.s: A drummer gets him a dance hall job at $25-30 a week; his mother consents if Uncle George sees him home.
279.q: Not at that time. I had not yet come in contact with anyone. This came later, after I played at this little theater down here. There was a drummer, who I must confess that my memory is just failing me a little bit at this point here, who was working at the Furn Dance Hall. And he met my father and…

279.t: Kids' commercial bands and first job at the St. Maurice Avenue theater
279.s: Early bands played collegiate arrangements, then a silent-movie trio at a dollar a night.
279.q: And I used to ride all the way from Lakeview to St. Maurice Avenue on a streetcar. And we got the big salary of a dollar a piece a night. But of course in those days, you know, a dollar was pretty good, you know. And for a couple of kids, I mean, it looked real good to us. And I guess money was…

279.t: First professional job in silent movie houses
279.s: Hug's first job was a three-piece group playing for silent films in neighborhood theaters.
279.q: When I first started, John, I would say that I played more so with little combinations. Like, for instance, you know, little groups, maybe three or four pieces. My first job, first professional job was in silent movie houses. That was with a three-piece group, drum, violin, and piano. And we played…

107.t: Jack Jackson's Jumping Jacks and Tom McClure's catchphrase
107.s: At about 14 he joined Jack Jackson's territory band alongside Matthew Garrett and Tom McClure, whose phrase 'and all such stuff as that' later became a song title.
107.ch: Cincinnati bands, race and the road to college
107.q: was a band under the leadership of a man named Jack Jackson, who was a saxophone player. He had this band called Jack Jackson’s Jumping Jacks. I played with men who were by far my senior. These were grown men. I was about 14 years of age, and I’m playing with guys in their 20s, 30s, 40s, and 50s.…

107.t: Charles Danzi's band and early dance gigs
107.s: His first group was a twelve-piece neighborhood band led by pianist Charles Danzi, playing teenage and young-adult dances in community centers and halls.
107.ch: Cincinnati bands, race and the road to college
107.q: But locally in the Walnut Hills area, which was referred to as one of the uptown suburbs, I became involved with a small dance band, about 12 pieces. I played alto saxophone with the band, and eventually I joined another band.

107.t: Starting to play at 11 and leading a band in high school
107.s: He began at 11, played semi-professionally from 13 and had a 12-piece band by senior year, all outside school.
107.q: Well I started off actually before my junior high years. My involvement was not with the school at all, just the junior high years I was performing on I guess you could say a semi- professional basis, from age 13. I actually started playing at age 11, and by age 17, well my senior year in high…

107.t: What his high school band earned
107.s: The 12-piece band got about $30 for a prom, with Foster taking three to five dollars.
107.q: Right $30. Which means that I would make about $5, $3 to $5, and the rest of the band would make $2 a piece.

64.t: First professional job at age 13 at the Howard Theater
64.s: At about 13 he covers for a pianist friend of his uncle at the Howard Theater, vouched for to his parents.
64.q: My first job was when I was about 13 years old. I had been playing, you know, like little high school and junior high school gigs and one of the people that I had met through my uncle was working at the Howard Theater and he needed someone to replace him. For some reason or another everybody was…

64.t: Playing teenage jobs on U Street
64.s: He played dances and accompanied singers in U Street clubs as an underage teenager, protected by his uncle and family reputation.
64.q: Basically I played kid stuff. I played for dances. Somebody would hire a band cheaply, just to entertain folks and go through that. But as I said, it was easy for me to work on U Street. My uncle knew all of the folks so he had taken me to hear some of these people and so they knew I was Bob…

64.t: Pickup gigs with young bands and the Baldwin and Miles orchestras
64.s: Young players like Johnny Malachi ran rehearsal bands hoping to sub with Bill Baldwin's or Tommy Miles's big bands, so he got called to sit in.
64.q: Just barely. Yeah, just… there were several young students or young men who had orchestras. Johnny Malachi had a band and a lot of young guys were… it was like a little rehearsal band but it was training for a hoped for gig with Bill Baldwin’s big band or Tommy Miles big band, which was fortunately…

64.t: First recitals, his mother's practice rules and a 75-cent dance job
64.s: His first performances were teacher recitals; his schoolteacher mother made him practice by repetition; his first paying jazz gig was a school dance for 75 cents.
64.q: Well my first performance was actually playing whatever little lessons we had had as piano students. And we played them primarily in the house of the music teacher. You know family and other people would come and then we might go to a small hall, nearby hall in the community and everybody would get…

494.t: First plane trip: Yusef Lateef in Detroit and The Centaur and the Phoenix
494.s: Subbing a matinee leads to the Minor Key in Detroit and an invitation to write and arrange for Yusef's Riverside session.
494.ch: Philadelphia roots and arrival in New York
494.q: Yeah. That was the year I graduated from high school. I worked in Philly at the Showboat. Yusef came through Philly, and his pianist missed the flight, because they had a matinee. We had a matinee in Philly. The matinee was like 4 o’clock. His pianist – I think his name was Abe, Abe Woodley –…

494.t: A week with Philly Joe Jones at the Showboat
494.s: Barron sits in for the pianist in Philly Joe's band alongside Bill, then is surprised by deductions from his pay.
494.ch: Philadelphia roots and arrival in New York
494.q: He came through Philadelphia. My brother was in the band at the time. I guess whoever – the pianist at the time was a gentleman – I think passed away now – a gentleman called Dick Katz. He was the pianist. Something happened. He wasn’t able to make it. So Bill told Philly Joe about his kid brother.…

494.t: Playing r-and-b dance gigs in Mel Melvin's band
494.s: The cabaret dances, shows and dancers Barron played for as a young teen in a small group with Bill.
494.ch: Philadelphia roots and arrival in New York
494.q: Yeah, basically, but rhythm-and-blues meant something totally different then. It really was music based on the blues and I Got Rhythm chords. Yeah, Rhythm and blues. That’s what it is. It was basically dance music, shuffles. It was basically dance music. We used to play at what was called cabarets.…

494.t: Working with Jimmy Heath and Sam Reed in Philly after-hours clubs
494.s: Introduced to Jimmy Heath, he plays his Really Big arrangements and after-hours shows around South Street.
494.ch: Philadelphia roots and arrival in New York
494.q: Jimmy I met when I was 17. I started working with him. He had just gotten out. That’s no secret. He tells everybody. He had gone to prison, and he had just gotten out. I met him. I was on South Street. I was working with a saxophonist named Sam Reed in Philly. He and Jimmy were very, very [?]. Sam…

470.t: The older Indianapolis musicians, Eldridge Morrison's band and transcribing Atomic Basie
470.s: Older players such as Roger Jones and Jimmy Coe; his first work was with Eldridge Morrison's band, for whom he transcribed Atomic Basie for $15 a chart.
470.ch: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
470.q: In the early 1900s, this is where Noble Sissle would have been plying his trade. There were all these clubs – again, a completely closed society. Later on Noble Sissle would team up with Eubie Blake to write the first important – I think – musical in this country, a musical called Shuffle Along in…

470.t: Playing professionally with Eldridge Morrison at the Indiana Roof
470.s: His first professional work with Eldridge Morrison in high school, including a laughing fit with Slide Hampton at the Indiana Roof.
470.ch: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
470.q: Oh yes, still in high school, and not a very good player, I might add, but then neither were most of the people either. I didn’t read well. I could read classical music, but when people started talking about cut time, I was still trying to beat my foot in 4, and it wouldn’t work. I’d be lost most…

470.t: Playing the junior prom and learning swing riffs
470.s: The Rhythm Rockets' disastrous junior prom, and learning simple riffs like Intermission Riff to start jamming.
470.ch: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
470.q: . . . with the Rhythm Rockets. That was a – I mean, we were a sad band. We played The Man I Love on blues changes. My dad worked at the post office. At 9 o’clock, the Columbia streetcar would pass Crispus Attucks High School going back out to the east side, so . . .

470.t: Sitting in at Indiana Avenue clubs as teenagers
470.s: Baker, Slide Hampton and other beginners sat in at jam sessions along Indiana Avenue alongside pros like Pookie Johnson, Jimmy Coe and the Montgomerys.
470.ch: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
470.q: All the clubs along Indiana Avenue [also known as "The Avenue"]. There must have been probably 20 clubs. Each of them had a jam session night. You would go – some of them had the same night. We would go from one club to another, playing our blues and then leave and go to the next club and play…

369.t: Her first big solo job at Costello's Grill
369.s: A friend's boy recommended her to the man downstairs and she got a solo gig at $60 a week.
369.q: Some of my mother’s friend’s boy told the man downstairs about me.

369.t: Playing with Bob Tinsley's dance band at the Swingland
369.s: The six or seven piece band played square music for two or three dollars; she gave her mother room-and-board money and tips were split by her mood.
369.q: Five, ten and one man gave us a dollar once. So I said, “Is this going three ways?”

369.t: The school High Jinx variety show
369.s: Captain Dyette booked all school talent into the High Jinx, a packed show paying a dollar a night until the principal stopped it; she played both classical and jazz.
369.q: Captain Dyette would take all the talent and book it on one day. And it was successful. And it was called the High Jinx. It would go two or three days.

369.t: Fellow High Jinx performers and the school band
369.s: Savannah Strong, Tommy Rigsby, Squeaky and dancer Raymond Sneed performed; she accompanied them in a ten-piece band with Dyette's arrangements.
369.q: Savannah Strong, Tommy Rigsby, Bert McCloskey, you know all local people. But they were very good.

86.t: Playing for experience in the Earl Hood band; mother demands pay
86.s: Hood did not pay him until his mother called and insisted, after she had bought the tuxedo.
86.q: tuxedo. So my mother bought me a tuxedo. And on weekends we’d go to all the little places around, I used to play a lot where the Mills Brothers were born in Pickaway, OH. We’d go to all the little neighboring places around Ohio and I never got paid. Most of them were getting 35 cents for the night…

86.t: Earl Hood's band: playing for experience, not pay
86.s: Paul Tyler brought him into Earl Hood's band; Hood paid nothing until Edison's mother threatened to see him.
86.q: fantastic saxophone player, he -- oh, Johnny Hodges knew him well, everybody, because he was really a good saxophone player. He moved next door to my mother and I used to play and play, you know, try to be a trumpet player. So he heard me one day he said -- he was playing with Earl Hood. He said,…

86.t: Earl Hood band: stock arrangements and his first solo on Limehouse Blues
86.s: At 14 he took his first solo when the other trumpeter was at the bar; he also remembers Bob Price.
86.q: It was just stock arrangements. We had two trumpets and a trombone and the other trumpet player, he used to play all the solos, play all the firsts and I was just sitting there. So, one night, we were playing at this Masonic Hall on Long Street and when his time came to play he was having a drink…

86.s: He joined a rich family's backed band with Sy Oliver, Jimmy Crawford and Joe Thomas, and went to Cleveland at fifteen or sixteen.
86.q: Oh, definitely. Definitely. And then I played -- went to school until there was a band called Morrison's Grenadiers. They formed a band around there with Sy Oliver, Jimmy Crawford, Joe Thomas --

90.t: Touring at twelve and playing pig stands
90.s: Summer tours with Doc Palmer at twelve, then Sunday pig-stand gigs working for tips that Doc split.
90.q: So I had the experience of working with these guys with Doc's band. That's what really got me on the road. We'd go out on tours during the summer, and it was a spectacular feat(?) at 12 years old going out on a tour, you know.

90.t: Bradley's nightclub across the Pearl River
90.s: Playing at Bradley's for fifty cents a night plus tips, learning to hear and make up tunes without written music.
90.q: And I also played at a place across the Pearl(?) River, the famous or ill-famed Pearl River, at a place called Bradley's with Doc Palmer. It was like... It had a filling station out in front, and a grocery store, and then a nightclub in the back. And we played in the nightclub part. And our basic…

90.t: Paul Gayten's Sizzling Six, Crystal Palace and WJDX broadcasts
90.s: He plays matinees with Paul Gayten's small group at the Crystal Palace and Savoy, broadcasts on WJDX, and hears visiting big bands.
90.q: : I was 14 when I joined that band. And then Paul Gayten put another little group together called Paul Gayten and His Sizzling Six. We had two saxophones. There was Duke Holliston, and Duke was playing tenor with this group. And we had a guitar player, a fine guitar player, who made some marks…

90.t: Leaving school for Detroit and the Bandbox
90.s: He leaves in the eleventh grade for his uncle's grocery in Detroit, and gets gigs at the Bandbox musicians' club where older players test him.
90.q: In fact, I left school in the Eleventh Grade. My Uncle, (?) Bernard(?) Reed and his wife, who was like my second mother, Lydia, they moved to Detroit. And as soon as he got himself going pretty well, anybody from home who wanted to come to Detroit, who figured they had a better chance...and he was…

430.t: First paid job with Johnny Prudhomme's band
430.s: His first job was a political rally with Johnny Prudhomme's band, paid a quarter plus beer and sandwiches.
430.q: No, I don't know, no. My first job was with Johnny Peronis' band. I got down the quarter for that. I don't know. We played a, that was a, what do you call it? One of those rallies. Somebody was running for something. I don't know. And that happened to be at Charter and, Charter and St. Rock. On the…

430.t: Buying first drum set and first job at a dollar and a quarter
430.s: Saving from his St. Charles Hotel job he bought drums; John Perdonce got him his first gig.
430.q: No, so I went to work at St. Charles Hotel. I was running the freight elevator there. And I get paid every two weeks. So my mother knew I wanted to set a drum, so she said, well, let's put the money aside. So at one time I had enough to make a down payment. So we go over to Glenwall, where my…

430.t: First professional job with Johnny Pernodon, about 1915
430.s: With $25 saved from a hotel job he bought drums and played a political job for Pernodon the same day, about 1915.
430.q: And that was my first job. To play professionally, you know. From then on, I went on up.

8.t: His first job at a house party
8.s: At about nine or ten he played bass at a house party with his brother and Caniniis Jackson and fell asleep on the bandstand.
8.q: I played a job and I, it was Caniniis Jackson. You love to go Caniniis Jackson? Caniniis Jackson played violin. While in the bass guitar? While in the bass. While in the bass. Well, he was playing guitar. My brother had to be on the bass. And John was playing his violin. Just three of us. A little…

8.t: First job at age nine for 25 cents
8.s: Johnny takes the nine-year-old to a house party where he falls asleep on the bass and is paid 25 cents.
8.q: He taken me out, and I laid the bass back on my shoulder, set in a chair, because I couldn't stand up to the bass, you know. I was only nine years old.

8.t: Turning professional in 1909 and the New Orleans bandleaders
8.s: Garland became professional in 1909, liked by bandleaders Perez, Dusen, Dawson and Robichaux, and played with the Eagle, Crescent, Imperial and Peerless bands.
8.q: Robichaux. They all -- they used to call me The Kid. "Let's get The Kid." All them bass players was coming over to me and stick me up on that stand, you understand, to play. And I played, and they'd shake their heads. I'm growing fast. And I was growing fast, if I have to say it myself. Done fine…

184.t: First job: filling in for Tubby on a Plaquemines Parish engagement
184.s: In short pants, borrowing long trousers, he substituted for his brother with a band playing below New Orleans and was hired from then on.
184.q: Yeah, in the country. No, he used to play in brass band. Up there, they had a brass band? Yeah, yeah, one of them in Yolens, Louisiana brass band. So I don't know how my brother started, but he gave me these sticks. So that's how I picked it up myself. So my first plane was, he used to work for…

184.t: First three-piece band with Arthur Campbell and Sidney Bechet
184.s: His first job was upstairs at a nightclub on Gravier Alley in a trio with pianist Arthur Campbell and Sidney Bechet.
184.q: Oh yeah, they used to call me Little Tubby. So that's what started me to play him. So finally when I, the first band that I, it was a three piece band, a fellow by the name, Arthur Campbell, I'm a piano player, I don't know if you've ever heard of him. I've heard of him, yes. Arthur Campbell and…

184.t: How he got the nickname Ram and first sat in with Kid Ory
184.s: Hall explains the nickname Kid Ory gave him and how he first played with Ory at St. Catherine Hall, substituting for Ory's drummer Henry Martin.
184.q: Alright, let's go ahead. Do you want to give me a name first? Well, my right name is Minor Hall. And as far as this rhyme is concerned, Kid already gave me that nickname.

641.t: Turning professional at sixteen; reading music in Tuts Johnson's band
641.s: He and his brother had a band at 14; he was a pro at 16 charging two or three dollars a gig, and the Tuts Johnson players all read music.
641.q: Well, my brother and I started, had a band when I was about, uh, fourteen years old. We used to play parties, and we played. Where did your brother play? Violin.

641.t: First paid jobs as a teenage pupil
641.s: Roque and Buddy Petit sometimes took him on jobs at 14 or 15 for a dollar or two while bands earned three to five dollars.
641.ch: Instruments, first jobs and the regional scene
641.q: It's according to the size of the crowd, yeah. A lot of times they played percentage deals. But I think when they played... They would play for as cheap as three dollars, and when I went with them sometimes they would give me a dollar, or give me two dollars

641.t: Joining the Martel band in 1924 at five dollars a night
641.s: Joe and his brother hired Bert and Dayton Martel for a three-day convention job, then Albert Martel hired Joe as clarinetist at five dollars a night and he left the shoe shop.
641.q: Martel. And my brother got this job to pay for this Catholic Knights of ...(?)... Convention, but we only could get together three pieces, I remember. We had a banjo and we had drums, and myself and my brother, which played the violin. And he knew Bert, the trumpet player; he had met him someplace…

571.t: First job in 1914 with the Black Eagle band across the lake
571.s: George recalls his first job on St. Joseph's night 1914 with a small band, naming its members and the two-dollar pay.

571.s: Lewis says he played a few jobs with Punch and worked in Georgia Boyd's place, and played with nearly every New Orleans band off and on, including a brass band led by Allen's father.

571.t: Choice of reed and learning stiff reeds playing funerals
571.s: He buys La Vore reeds and learned to like stiff reeds playing funeral parades before taking up E-flat clarinet; Joe Watson is mentioned.
571.q: What is that? I lay your reed lavore. Lavore? It's supposed to be French. Well, all the reeds are supposed to be French. Sometimes I get a vibrator. I usually use a... I get a name reed. That ain't important, but I use it. That reed was my foist reed. But I always like the stiff reed. Because of…

270.t: Music store job and first professional band in Pensacola
270.s: Includes working at a music store and playing first jobs with married men, backed by Black fraternal organizations in Pensacola.
270.q: Well I wasn't calling myself a professional before, before 24. I was in ninth grade, 35, right there, F1-0. And these two guys was taking lessons. This man and these guys were married men and everything. They left in the days first. The Trammer played George Morris, and Trump was played Thomas…

270.t: The All-Star band and leaving for Pensacola
270.s: His teen band under George Morris rehearsed together, took drummer Joe Wynn, and left for a Pensacola baseball park job in April 1924.
270.q: Well, no. Like I said, this little, this band, they were all fellows older than me because I was just about 18, if I remember well. And they were all the trombone players named George Morris and the trombone players named Thomas Mack. And the clarinet player was named Edmund Washington.

270.t: Early jobs in Polyland and on the riverfront, then leaving for Pensacola with Joe Wynn
270.s: The young band plays a rough Prohibition-era place in Polyland and a foundry office during a strike, then in April 1924 Joe Wynn recruits them for Pensacola despite his mother's objections, leaving cousin Pete behind.
270.ch: Learning violin and banjo in New Orleans
270.q: yeah so uh like I said we were rehearsing with these Mac Thomas Mac George Morris and Edmund Hall you see and uh we used to play out this place the colored place out in Polyland this is during Prohibition now and I remember we had numbers like uh uh what were you that those days you played you had…

58.s: Miller recalls his first paid night playing blues for fifty cents and half-remembered musicians he met.

58.t: Early pay in New Orleans and Raceland
58.s: Punch recalls his first New Orleans job pay and playing for tips on a store gallery in Raceland.
58.q: Oh yeah we'd make, like, me and this boy they called Lonnie Johnson now, we called him Rooster at home, but we'd play on Saturday evening on a big store gallery you see, and put our hat down and all the people that's playing put money in our hat see, we didn't have no siren or nothing like that.…

58.t: First bands in New Orleans: Duck Ernest and Jack Carey
58.s: Miller recalls his boyhood friend who played alto and then lists Duck Ernest and Jack Carey as his first bands, with Carey for dance music.
58.q: I was raised with him. What was he? What did he play? He played alto. We was in the army together and I learned bugle and I learned bugle. And did he play in any bands? Well he played in any band we had out there in the country, you know, brass bands.

105.t: Snare drum to full kit, and professional work instead of school music
105.s: Brown asks about moving from snare to kit; Hamilton says he played no music at school, worked gigs from age 15 or 16, and out-earned his father at about $27 a week.
105.q: I only played in the band, marching band, one semester and I told you why, just to get my sweater, you know. In the meantime man, I’m working, I’m playing the joints.

105.t: Roadhouse gigs with Old Man Meyers and a rodeo
105.s: Playing for seventy-five cents in Meyers's all-colored orchestra, and a bull loose at a rodeo.
105.q: Hey man you know, speaking of that, we had this — there was a band. There was a man, a gentleman in L.A., his name was Meyers. And we used to call him Old Man Meyers. Jack and I used to play with him in his orchestra. He had I think three sons, one played piano, one played trumpet and one played I…

105.t: Subbing at the Club Alabam, playing for strippers, and three weeks with Hampton
105.s: Jo told him to stay in school; he subbed for Lee Young at the Club Alabam, learned to play strip-show kicks at the Follies, and Lionel Hampton hired him at 16 but let him go after three weeks because he could not read.
105.q: Stay in school. He told me to stay in school, you know, and that was cool. So in the meantime, Lee was playing with Lorenzo Flennoy and they were playing at the Club Alabam, which was the number one club there, which was equivalent to the Cotton Club here in New York. 68.t: Miss Callie Frost's audition and a busy schedule, about 1927
68.s: A college-connected patron hears the family band, and the group gets three or four gigs a week; Tate is 12 or 13.
68.ch: Family band and learning to play

This is where we all started and these are the ones. Thank God they're still hanging in there, you know?" And there was a…

68.t: Lonnie Johnson pays $50 each, which settles Tate on music
68.s: Johnson pays each player fifty dollars, which convinces Tate to become a musician; he later saw Johnson in Toronto.
68.ch: Family band and learning to play
68.q: playing, he calls me over into the corner -- I don't know why he chose me -- he says -- he gave me $50.00. In those days, the dollar bills were much larger than now and fifty, it looked like you had a thousand.

68.s: Tate sketches his path: family band in Sherman, T. Holder's Clouds of Joy, Victoria Spivey, Lester Young, Millinder, Goodman, 21 years at the Celebrity Club.

672.s: Before John Levy and Cannonball she sang at fifteen with Sir Raleigh Randolph's Sultans of Swing, then with Rusty Bryant's band, and had a TV show.

672.s: Sent to a talent contest for her high school, she was offered a twice-weekly TV show with a taciturn pianist.

672.t: Working Columbus nightclubs and the Sultans of Swing
672.s: As a teenager she worked Club Regal and other rooms, sang with Sir Wally Randolph's big band, and was protected by the musicians.
672.q: I performed pretty much at every nightclub. One that I stayed at a long time was called Club Regal. I worked on weekends there. I worked just about every place you could work in Columbus.

368.t: Pay with Scat Davis and young pianist Dodo Marmarosa
368.s: He earned $75 a week with Davis and met Dodo Marmarosa, who joined at fourteen.
368.q: I met a lot of guys that I played with later, like Dodo Marmaroso was a well- known young fellow. He wasn’t, in fact, when he joined Johnnie “Scat” Davis, he was fourteen years old.

368.s: As a teenager he played in a kids' big band with Al Alberts and Joe Wilder at block parties and on radio.

368.t: Philadelphia after-hours clubs and being discovered by Scat Davis
368.s: Billy Krechmer and Nat Siegel ran after-hours clubs where he sat in; Johnnie Scat Davis offered him a road job.

110.t: Entering the Stockton musicians union and scale wages
110.s: Brubeck, a freshman nobody knew, is brought into the union by Herman Shapiro, lands a $42-a-week club job and earns more than his future father-in-law.
110.ch: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years

110.s: At about 14 he is invited to play a dance on the Mokelumne River, where rancher Loren Beimert sings, and he describes stock arrangements.

110.s: He opens, plays intermission and escorts the well-known pianist Cleo Brown, at about age 19.

565.s: At about 17 he got a booking with his own young band at Sunnyside Gardens, but had to change his name.

9.t: First gigs: a five-dollar dance and the stranded Watson show
9.s: A first gig had a pianist who knew only two keys; then a singer Watson's show band collapsed in Leominster and left them stranded overnight.
9.ch: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs

9.t: Hodges offered a place with a burlesque show
9.s: Eddie Haywood's father tried to take Hodges on the road; shy Hodges asked Holmes along, who refused, and Holmes met many big-time musicians through Hodges.
9.ch: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
9.q: : Yes, of course. Eddie Haywood's daddy, he was playing a show that was a burlesque show, and he tried to get Johnny to go with him. But see, Johnny didn't read music at the time. 9.ch: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
9.q: : No. I met Joe Steele in church. His sister was my Sunday School teacher. I was going to Sunday School in them days, as a little boy. His mother... They were very religious people. Yeah, I met Joe in church.

381.t: First house-party gig with Bella Roberts
381.s: His first gig at about eleven was a house party with Bella Roberts on trumpet, Gladys Roberts on piano and Milton Fletcher on bass.
381.ch: Teenage bands and Florida road tours
381.q: Well, I got into jazz playing house parties. Yeah. See, they used to have a lot of house parties in Miami, I mean, everybody used to give a party there on a Saturday, and so that was how I got the chance to start playing house parties.

381.t: First gig in 1931 and the barbecue-stand juke joint
381.s: His first gig was at the UNIA Hall in July 1931; then Sonny Boy hired him for a rough juke joint where the band hid behind the piano.
381.ch: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
381.q: So I played, between the UNIA Marching Band and St. Agnes Marching Band, I played with these two until I reached the age of around 12½.

381.t: Becoming the family meal ticket and the Barbecue Stand
381.s: After his parents separated, his mother put him to work; at twelve he played four nights a week in a rough barbecue joint, ducking behind the piano during shootings.
381.ch: Teenage bands and Florida road tours
381.q: Yep, Bella Roberts. So that was my first time that I remember playing. But then my mother found out that I had a natural talent for the drums, and at this time, they had separated -- they separated when I was around 11 years old. And that's when I became the meal ticket.

382.s: Her uncle Harry led a band in Homestead that recorded on Gennett and let her sing; through him she got a first job.

120.t: The Ohio Lucky Seven and the armory dances
120.s: A manager rents small-town armories for the kid band to run its own dances, and each member takes home about $30 a weekend, which wins over his grandparents.

120.t: Joining the Chubb-Steinberg band under Art Hicks
120.s: The band is owned by two music-store men; leader Art Hicks offers $50 a week and he joins at Bond Hill House, his first recording band for Okeh.
120.q: Yeah - Chubb - Steinberg--- and this was a band owned by two men who had a music store in Cincinnati and everybody thought that this ChubbSteinberg was one guy's name - but it was really two. Chubb and Steinberg.

120.t: Roland Potter's Peerless Players at Bowling Green
120.s: At seventeen he leaves home to join a college-dance band at Bowling Green and works hard to learn its arrangements.

117.t: First professional job at Sheboygan Inn on C-Melody
117.s: At sixteen Freeman gets a C-Melody and two years later plays the Sheboygan Inn in Lyman Woods's trio on Dave Tough's recommendation, barely able to play.

117.q: Frank Tesch Teschemacher and I were close, we went to Austin High School together, and we had -- I was still playing the C-Melody saxophone and we had a sort of sax team and we would do -- were playing professionally now and getting as much as we could, we weren't really good enough to get -- to…

117.t: Dave Tough leaves, Freeman is fired and switches to tenor
117.s: Earning $40 a week, Freeman is threatened with murder after Tough leaves, returns to Chicago and takes up tenor, relearning in B-flat by ear.
117.q: All right. 427.t: Jessie the barmaid and trying to get on the bandstand
427.s: Washing glasses for the Italians, he sat by barmaid Jessie and was thrown out whenever he asked the bands to let him sing.

6.t: First gigs with Willy Freeman's band, playing stocks
6.s: A Commerce High schoolmate, Willy Freeman, brought him into a local band playing stock arrangements at places like the Renaissance Casino for $12 a job.

6.s: He played a Prohibition-era gangster roadhouse in Albany in a small band with drummer Jimmy Campbell, later joined by Johnny Russell, and learned from the older pianist Paddy Armstead.

6.t: Joining Sapiro's band at the Bamboo Inn
6.s: He walked into the Chinese-restaurant nightclub and got the saxophone job, his first band with special arrangements; he lists sidemen including Joe Garland, Manzie Johnson, Jimmy Archey and Freddy Johnson, and the club soon folded.
6.ch: Dancing schools, Sapiro and Jelly Roll Morton

125.t: Carthage, Missouri at fourteen: shoeshine boy popping his rag
125.s: Wanting extra money for clothes, he shined shoes at a hotel barbershop and added musical rag-popping that earned bigger tips.

125.s: At fourteen he also washed cars and was a bellboy, earning tips and a local name as an entertainer with his ukulele.

79.t: Two older men ask him to play cornet in a roadhouse
79.s: Roadhouses outside Webster Groves were run by families. Two men who knew his family came to hire Joe to play cornet.
79.ch: Boyhood in Webster Groves and early roadhouse work

79.t: Capitol dedication; Rankin's gigs and campus dances
79.s: Thomas got three days off for the dedication. Bud Rankin got him good jobs paying $8 to $10, and he played dances for seniors and with Mr. Jefferies.

768.t: Joining the New Orleans band at a Chinese restaurant
768.s: A New Orleans band (Garland, Palmer, Dewey, Sugar Johnny, Tubby Hall) tried her out, and she joined at $27.50 a week without telling her mother.

768.t: Demonstrating sheet music at Jones Music Store
768.s: Soon after arriving in Chicago in 1918 she got a job playing songs at a State Street music store, learning the stock and drawing crowds.
768.q: Oh, it was, um, well, we moved here the last part of, uh, 1918. And, um, I was to go back to school the following, uh, September. In the meantime, I went down State Street one day, and I passed this music store, with all this music in the window, so I went in and asked the lady for a song, that I…

769.t: First professional job with George Lewis
769.s: Playing with Lewis was his first professional work; earlier jobs paid about five dollars.
769.q: After George took me on his wing, then we started making a little more money, you know. Yeah. Did you just- Well, at that time, George's popularity was growing then too.

769.t: First jobs: trio in a Gentilly barn and the Silver Star
769.s: Herbert Moran urges him to keep drumming; the trio with Walter Nelson plays a barn job, then the Silver Star nightclub with hired sidemen.
769.q: Oh, that was around in the 1940s. Yeah, in the 1940s, because I was living across the street at the time, at 825 North Galvestre. And the first job that, after he found out that I was playing that good, Herbert Moran, one of our old time trumpet men, he was a wonderful jazz man on the trumpet. He…

248.t: Leaving the lumber yard for Canadian Jackson's band
248.s: Dawson says no one else in his family played; he left a lumber yard when Cornelius Jackson offered work, earned twenty-two dollars the first night, and later ran his own band at Harry Parker's.
248.ch: Fish fries, passing the hat and district living
248.q: You had nothing to do, didn't you? I started when, with a guitar, you know, just like I told you, people sometimes, bands used to serenade, you see. They'd go around people's house like that and serenade them late at night, wake them up.

248.t: Dawson's first job at Rice's with Kenneas Jackson
248.s: He played fish fries as a one-man band, then Jackson hired him at Rice's across from Pete Lala's, paying far above his sawmill wage.
248.q: Uh, let's see, I, I couldn't, let me first job, let's see. Oh yeah, first job, I'll tell you my first job. Our first job was with Kenneas Jackson. I played guitar. I was working at Thompson Sawmill. Where was that? Broad and Portis. I was working, working at Thompson Sawmill and I could play…

999.t: Working out his ages and dates
999.s: They date the kazoo band, Willie Parker and Kid Howard to about age 19 to 23.
999.q: That was my first job, I played both drums. What caused that, because Howard had two jobs that night and he didn't want to let the jobs go see. Let Harrison take that band, take that charge of that job and he went on down to Grand Island and play. That's where he got to go down to Grand Island that…

999.t: His first jobs and the kazoo band
999.s: He restates his first orchestra job with Harrison Verrett and Homer Eugene and his first brass-band job with Willie Parker, and the kazoo band.
999.q: Yeah, with Harrison Verrett Hall, Homer Eugenie and myself. But my first job on the street on a brass band was with Willie Parker. He's the first man brought me on the street.

255.t: Morris French, the legless pianist Penny, and jam sessions
255.s: Older trumpeter Morris French and pianist Penny, who lost his legs at Lutcher, played that first job; the young players also went out jamming to get hired.
255.ch: First jobs and New Orleans players
255.q: Great tramp-owner. Great tramp-owner player. And I had him there, start out with, because I always take the older fellow with me on everything, because I figured like that, well, he knew. Yeah. You ought to have somebody as a guide, you know. Well, I took him, and another fellow played piano by the…

255.t: First bands and the first job at the Gypsy Tea Room
255.s: He names bands he played in and recalls his first job, six months after getting the horn, where older players made him put the music away.
255.ch: First jobs and New Orleans players
255.q: The first job I played, to tell you the positive, the truth, was about six months after I got the horn. I played a job. Oh, yeah. And the first job I played was down in the Gypsy Tea Room. Oh, yeah. Down on Royal Street. They had a Gypsy Tea Room was down there. And the people was head that day,…

21.t: Ike Jackson offers him a job at McIschus's saloon
21.s: While advertising on a wagon he is spotted by bassist Ike Jackson, who offers him a nightly job at a saloon in the district.
21.ch: Picnics, wagon advertising and saloon work
21.q: Oh, no. Oh, no. So, from Jack Kerris, we were playing once, an advertisement on a Sunday, for a dance over in Gretna, while we'd play mostly every Sunday night, called the Come Clean. We'd make an advertisement on Sunday. On the wagon. On Monday. Yeah, on the wagon. So, I remember one Sunday, on…

21.t: First job on a pleasure boat, playing violin
21.s: His first paid job was on a Mississippi excursion boat playing violin in a small string and cornet group.
21.ch: Early life, family and Crescent Orchestra
21.q: What was the job? The job was on the, it was on a pleasure boat on the Mississippi River. Excursion? Yeah, pleasure boat ran from, say, Esplanade Street down Chalamet. Down below.

22.t: Free groups, 'no beer no music' bands, and his own band of 1918
22.s: He lists the downtown and uptown groups he played with for free, then taking outside jobs, picture shows, and having his tunes written down.
22.q: Susu Ramis played guitar Willie guitar played bass Harry Nunez played violin and I played the comic we played in the downtown section that is way down below Elysian Fields Avenue now this is 19 2 3 and 4 and 5 no night I made ahead I went ahead of my statement 19 3 4 and 5 and maybe 6 the uptown…

22.t: Early string bands and free serenades in the Irish Channel
22.s: He played professionally around 1908 after string bands in 1902-03, with the old high-pitch cornet and unpaid party jobs.
22.q: I had played in other little string bands before that, 1902, 1903, with small outfits that we'd go serenading around the Irish Channel.

191.t: The Melody Four, The Girl from Marshall movie and yama yama suits
191.s: Kelly's first paid band, the Melody Four, played in a hometown movie wearing yama yama clown suits.
191.q: Well, the Melody Four that I first played with in Marshall was composed of Jake Goldberg, a drummer, and Pye Atkins, James Atkins, excuse me, James Davis, Pye Davis, Piano, Tootie Buck ! Garrett, Clarinet, and me, saxophone. The first band I played with, for money, I played saxophone.

191.t: First paid jobs and leaving home to join Ham Crawford
191.s: He plays C-melody sax for $12.50, plays with small bands around Texas, runs off without permission, and joins Ham Crawford's band at sixteen.
191.q: Albert System clarinet is, of course, it's different from the band system clarinet, in that the band is an improved fingering mechanism. But, Albert is, I don't know, he just seemed to fall into it naturally. Easier to play by here, anybody who has, you'd say a little knack for it. But, I left…

878.t: First band with Pansy Lane and early jobs
878.s: Harry's first job was with Alfred 'Pansy' Lane, then the Pup Cafe and Raleigh Rye with Ed, before he quit to work for his father.
878.q: Alfred Lane. Alfred Lane. Alfred Lane. Called him Pansy Lane. I played with him before I played with Emmett. And then I worked with him a while playing prize fights around the street, you know, advertising rather. And we went to work at the old Pup Cafe on Ivorville Street and worked there a while.…

878.t: Larry's marching bands and Clem Camp
878.s: Harry says Laine gave many players their start, and tells of Larry in marching bands and the St. Francis de Sales Band with clarinetist Clem Camp.
878.ch: Larry Shields and the Dixieland Band
878.q: Well, I imagine Jack just about gave all these guys their first start in the music business. And of course I've had quite a few to tell me that, such as Nick LaRocka, Larry. But Larry played with quite a few bands around here before he left, he played with the marching bands, you know, and played…

195.t: How he got on with Bill Boyd and Blackie Simmons; the band's teasing
195.s: He sat in on radio and dance jobs with Bill Boyd's Cowboy Ramblers and then filled in for Blackie's pianist. The country musicians liked his blues playing and enjoyed teasing him for his naivete.
195.q: Well, I had been playing a few radio programs and dance jobs with Bill Boyd's Cowboy Ramblers. And he had already made arrangements to hire the pianist from Blackie Simmons, but liked my work better. I've forgotten Sonny somebody. He's that first one who made the first records with Bill Boyd. But…

195.t: Joining Blackie Simmons' hillbilly band in 1935
195.s: Straight out of high school he joined Blackie Simmons' small band, playing honky-tonks and cheap dances. The pay was split by cuts, from about $8 to $30 a week. He dates this to 1935, then 1936 with the Doughboys.
195.q: Um, and... Yes, I joined the, uh, little hillbilly band, Blackie Simmons. And Blackie Simmons saw Duke Ellington's bus pass by one time. They said, Duke Ellington's famous bus. Famous, Duke Ellington's famous orchestra. That's a famous orchestra all outside of the bus. And he had had Blackie's blue…

780.t: First band in high school and radio spot on Dr. Daniel's show
780.s: In 1951 he formed an eight-piece school band that began at the Shadowland and played Saturday radio on WMRY.
780.q: When I was going to school, I was in high school when, let's see, in 1951, I think. I think, I think, yeah, it was 1951.

780.t: Still in school, the band as a bunch of kids
780.s: He was still in school and living with his parents at about 16; the drummer was the youngest at 14.
780.q: I know I was 16. I had to be 16. I graduated from school when I was 17. So I must have been 16 or younger. I was real young.

118.t: First professional job and Lawrence Toca
118.s: At about twelve he played with his cousin Lawrence Marrero around Franklin and Charters; also jobs with trumpeter Toca.
118.q: The first job I played, I'll tell you what, I was about 12 years old when I played my first professional job. That was Lawrence Morell, my cousin. You remember Lawrence Morell? Oh yeah. Yeah, well Lawrence was one of the fellas, you know. Well me and Lawrence, sometime we used to hide his fellas,…

118.t: First jobs, Bunk Johnson and the kazoo band
118.s: Early jobs with Norman Blaze and Cornbread, a wartime gig with Bunk Johnson, Papa Celestine, the kazoo band and house parties.
118.q: Well, I played jobs, I played jobs with boys like, uh, well, they were men over me, but I was quite young. They was, uh, like Euleth John. Like I first said, I played jobs with, uh, Norman Blaze, which was a drummer. I mean, he never played a job on Bowman Street before in his life. I'm more than…

153.t: First professional gig in Rock Island for $3
153.s: His first job was a piano, trumpet and drums trio with no bass, at about 14, playing Ellington, Basie and Hampton material for three dollars.
153.q: Yeah. It was in Rock Island, Illinois. The gig was a piano player, a trumpet player, and drums. That’s all. No bass. What an odd combination. But they were all good players. So I had to supply what the piano player and bass player would play, as well as doing what I did on my drum set. The trumpet…

153.t: Joining the union at fourteen and sitting in with Spec Red's quartet in Moline
153.s: He joined the Moline union at fourteen, played with a chaperone, and learned swing sitting in on Tuesdays with a quartet at the Rendezvous.
153.q: Well I was very fortunate, they allowed me to join the union in Moline, Illinois when I was fourteen years old. However, in order to play the gigs at that time, you had to play in a little beer joint you know, I had to be accompanied by a grown up. They had to get me there, help me set up the drums…

537.t: First night with Papa French's band, 1976
537.s: Sent to substitute for his father, he is made bandleader by Papa French and calls tunes like Milenberg Joys.
537.q: Yeah. It was very nice to see him. I told him all about that. He was like, me? I said yeah, you. But in 1976 Albert Papa French, who took over the band from Papa Celestin, which was like the oldest established band in the world, continuing like from 1910, he called my dad to make a job. And my dad…

537.t: Vladimir Vasiliev, the 500 Club and the Aquarians
537.s: Through Herlin Riley he gets a strip-club job on Bourbon Street under Vladimir Vasiliev and joins his Latin band the Aquarians.
537.q: The drummer? He and I grew up like brothers. I mean I was the best man in his wedding. And he came in Sears one day and he says, “Hey what are you doing working here, man?” I said, “Well it’s part of my college course and I have to do it.” He says, “Look I’m working a job on Bourbon Street as a…

807.s: He faked the solo from the melody's outline, played with that band for years, and was paid about $18.
807.q: No he said, “Can you play a solo?” And I said, “Well if somebody else plays first.” Because the wheels were turning for me, right? You know? And I don’t know why but they were — I said well I’m going to figure out. So I heard it and I said, “Wait, I can play that, that’s in C, the beginning of it.”…

807.t: First job at 14: 'Perdido' in B flat
807.s: At 14 he was called to a local party house band, handed 'Perdido' in B flat, and transposed from a C fake book.
807.q: Yeah. My first job was when I was 14. Okay? With older musicians. Because I lived about 400 yards from an American Legion — no it wasn’t an American Legion — it was like one of those little party houses. Not a big one, just a little one. And they would have weddings in there and you know the…

518.t: Father strolling with violin; gigs at fourteen with brother Bob
518.s: His brother drove him to big-band gigs at fourteen, he joined the union and played every night.
518.q: My brother may have, since he’s eight years older than me. I did not. But I did — he would take me to gigs when I was fourteen, playing with the big band. I’d be like playing fourth, I was thrilled to death to be there. I couldn’t drive yet, and he would drive me there and he’d sit at the bar and…

518.t: Playing the Paderewski's supper club in Cleveland
518.s: At sixteen he took over the trumpet-and-rhythm gig at Paderewski's, and substituted wrong bridges to a pianist who couldn't improvise.
518.q: Of course. You have to come back to make some sense to it, you don’t want them to leave if you’re playing a live concert, a live performance. You know it’s like, and growing up I played in Cleveland, and I played in this one band it was called, well the club was called — well the club was called…

560.t: Fort Lauderdale's first mixed band and Cannonball on the street dance
560.s: Longo's father hired Cannonball for a street dance, the first mixed band in town; Cannonball's playing melted the crowd and led to the Harold Ferguson Band.
560.q: Yeah. And so I hired him for the gig, and as soon as he walked on the bandstand, the street was all filled. It was a street dance. There was a big hush that came over the audience you know. But as soon as he started playing “The Stars Fell on Alabama” it melted everybody’s heart and everybody…

560.t: Pay and the decision about college
560.s: He made about ten dollars a night, and his parents insisted he go to college rather than just play.
560.q: Oh, ten dollars or something like that. That was considered a lot of money back then.

721.t: First studio work: jingles in Dallas
721.s: He began recording jingles twice a week in Dallas while at North Texas State, doing eight to ten commercials an hour.
721.q: Wow. I started recording in Dallas when I was in college at North Texas State. Somehow somebody got my name and I started going into Dallas twice a week to record on jingles with the top professionals there in town. It was — we would do eight or ten commercials during a one-hour session. That means…

721.t: Lead trumpet with Brenda Lee and hitchhiking home
721.s: Rowe reads an anecdote about a six-night gig in Jackson paying $16; Malone recalls his father's advice to wear a suit.
721.q: Yes. My father told me if you’re going to hitchhike wear a suit. So I had to wear a suit to the gig anyway so — but nobody picked me up until the sun came out.

342.t: Playing R&B with Uncle Cookie at the Horseshoe
342.s: At 16 he played with Uncle Cookie's Seven Sharps at a segregated all-black Springfield club, skipping school and earning less than with his father.
342.ch: Family and early playing in Springfield
342.q: A swing and something Latin which was always [scats] — it was just terrible. I never heard or seen a Latin band, but I heard it on the radio and everything. And so I did that and then my Uncle Cookie, who had a band called the Seven Sharps, this was when I was in high school, I was 16 then, and I…

342.t: Uncle Gilley Roberts and the trad band
342.s: His 104-year-old uncle Gilley Roberts played banjo with Louis Armstrong; Marshall played in a trad band at colleges in the fifties.
342.q: RPI. I have an uncle who is still living, Gilley Roberts, he’s a banjo player who played with Louis Armstrong in 1927, and went to Europe with him and everything. Gilley is 104. And one of my other jobs, he was in the family too, it was another band I played in, we had a traditional jazz band. And…

113.t: First gig: playing two tunes over and over at a party
113.s: Asked to play a party with only two tunes, he repeated them all night, got paid and decided to learn more.
113.q: Well some guy was looking for a piano player, someone to play a party for him. He was having a party one night, and he couldn’t find nobody. So finally one guy told him he says, “Well old Mac up there” he says, “I don’t know how many tunes or songs he knows, but” he says, “I hear him plunking…

113.t: Sitting in with Al Dennie's band in Tulsa
113.s: Following the sound of a band rehearsing, he volunteered as pianist for Al Dennie's 12-piece band, who thought he could read and fake.
113.ch: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
113.q: Yes, this was during the Depression. And so one day, I heard a band playing and heard the music. So I followed the music, you know, kept following the sound. Kept following it until I came to a place and I could tell the band

811.s: Paid $36 in seventh grade on a TV show with a pizza parlor Dixieland band, joining the union and buying hi-hats.
811.q: $4? Yeah. And this was actually on a TV show with the local pizza parlor Dixieland band. And so it went through the union too. I had to become a union member, so it had taxes taken out of it and everything.

811.t: Playing club dates and jazz standards as a teenager in Ann Arbor
811.s: From age 14 he played dance gigs of standards, bossa novas and Dixieland at a pizza place; a pause to turn off the heater.
811.q: Yeah, but see when I was growing up, in the 60s and 70s, and probably you too, I had all this jazz coming at me and I was playing gigs starting at age 14, playing dance gigs on the weekend. And it was mostly jazz. We played three rock songs.

215.t: Watching big bands at the Paterson armory; early gigs in high school
215.s: Wartime troops at the armory, seeing Glen Gray, Jerry Wald and Stan Kenton, hating shop class, and earning a few dollars at weddings.
215.q: And then we also had a big armory in Paterson that would house the troops that were guarding the factories in Paterson. We had the Wright Aeronautical Company made airplane engines, and they were going like four years without stopping, just a roar. And they put artillery up on the mountains…

215.t: Joining Vaughn Monroe from high school; first road trip
215.s: With bands losing men to the draft, a friend called Bucky to fill a chair with Vaughn Monroe over Christmas vacation; his father's fifteen dollars and a ten-week theater tour after graduation.
215.q: Well they were in a way because my mother’s brothers were on the road — a brother was on the road — with a lot of different bands, Clyde McCoy, Buddy Rodgers, Raymond Scott, Teddy Powell, played with all the bands, played just rhythm but he was very good at it. Bob Chester. And I was on Christmas…

450.s: At 17 she joined her family in Scotland, then took a London club job for seven pounds ten a week, singing standards with a band.
450.q: And then I stayed a couple of weeks and went down to London. I got a job in a club, bought a second-hand dress and I thought I’d died and gone to heaven.

450.t: Leaving for Brighton and singing in a London private club
450.s: Her father gives her money and she goes to her uncle in Brighton; she auditions for a bandleader and sings with a ten-piece band in a snobbish private club, then reads for Jack Hylton's show Burlesque.
450.q: the carpet, and he lifted up a board. That’s where he kept his money. He gave me about £30. He said, “Let me call your mother’s brother. He lives in Brighton,” which is a seaside town, outside of London. So he called, and my uncle Bill said, “Okay, fine. She can come and stay with me and my wife.…

463.t: First live jazz band at Hamilton: Kaminsky, Mole, Pops Foster
463.s: He describes the New York group that came to Clinton around 1948, the first real jazz band he heard live.
463.q: Yeah, there was that one concert which I think was 19 — it was in the winter of 1948 — I could be mistaken, it might be ‘47, I’m not sure. But right in there, ‘46, ‘47, ‘48, when a group came up from New York City and I remember who they were very distinctly because I sort of had my eye out for…

463.t: Eli's Chosen Six and Buell Neidlinger
463.s: He played with the Yale Dixieland band a year before enrolling, brought in by bassist Buell Neidlinger.
463.q: Eli’s Chosen Six. I was playing with them a year before I actually went to Yale, because I knew some of the people in there. There was a bass player named Buell Neidlinger, and you might know his name from some of the stuff he did with Cecil Taylor and other

60.t: First gigs and the National Guard in Washington
60.s: Playing in a La Crosse bar, a Mauston band-director gig, and being called up in 1961 to Ft. Lewis.
60.ch: Early playing and the Riverboat Ramblers
60.q: Well you know I don’t even know. I don’t remember that. I don’t think there’s any problem. I mean they had their own things they were doing and it didn’t bother me. I would play once a week in a little bar in La Crosse for nothing and all the beer you can drink type thing, but it was fun and that…

60.s: With Charlie Marshall he formed a band that played every style of traditional jazz.
60.ch: Early playing and the Riverboat Ramblers
60.q: records and stuff, so we started to put together a little band called the Riverboat Ramblers, which it’s still going in Wisconsin, that started in ‘61. And I sort of cut my teeth on that, playing everything. We didn’t play the west coast style, which is the traditional, which is banjo, tuba and…

947.t: Gigs with the band: school dances, the hockey arena and union scale
947.s: Music gave him a social place in high school; he describes dances and Saturday gigs at the Fort William Gardens, $24 scale, and joining the union through Rocky Albertini.
947.q: Sure. I guess certainly it did, thinking back to high school days and stuff. But being in a band as it were wasn’t quite the same up in Fort William, Ontario.

947.t: School assemblies in Fort William: playing 'Pipeline' and meeting Rick Lazar
947.s: Shaffer joined the musicians union at 15, played piano at school assemblies, brought the house down with 'Pipeline', and was invited into Rick Lazar's band.
947.q: 15 years old so I’m just trying to place what year I might have been in high school. At some point in high school. Tenth grade or something.

423.t: Early struggle and getting started at seventeen
423.s: Ed worked at the phone company until about seventeen and a half, joined the union, then toured with Randy Brooks and Bobby Byrne before Ventura.
423.ch: Rock, Tonight Show and early career
423.q: Well I’m a very lucky guy because the only time that I had that was in the beginning. I worked at the phone company, I’d had a couple of day jobs, and I only worked a few gigs at night, and I can honestly tell you that from the age of less than 18, about 17-1/2, I was earning a living at music. It…

423.t: Learning on the road in Grade Z bands
423.s: Out of high school at 16, by 17 he was on band buses with lesser bands, working up the alphabet toward the Dorseys, Goodman, Basie and Ellington, helped by older musicians.
423.q: Oh, no. Well I graduated high school, I was 16, and by 17 I was on a band bus working with like Grade Z bands, you know—

823.t: First club-date jobs as a teenager in Connecticut
823.s: His father steered him away from kid bands toward older club-date players, who used him because he knew many tunes.
823.q: I guess I was between my junior and senior year I would say. I got the chance to play — one thing my dad did right, there was a lot of kid bands that were made up in the high school, Policeman’s Benevolent Association dances and little quasi-Dixieland bands that

823.s: He started earning weekend money in high school as the only New London trombonist who could play Dixieland, learning ensemble roles.
823.q: Actually I started playing professionally up in Connecticut when I was in high school. That’s really where I basically started. I started making 25, maybe 50 bucks on the weekend.

219.t: Playing Boston sailor joints as a teenager
219.s: His parents waited in the car while he played rough joints, learning by ear.
219.q: I had no direction. I was a kid playing the piano. I mean my folks would pick me up at one o’clock in the morning when I was playing some of these joints, and I mean they were joints. I mean I would play in joints. And they would be out in the car waiting for me. I was sixteen or seventeen years,…

219.t: Grant Wilson and his Stardusters, a teenage cellar band
219.s: Wein explains the stage name and the cellar band, and says he was an organizer who called people up to make things happen.
219.q: Well, I, in those days, you know, it was the days before Simon and Garfunkle, you know, so people changed their names, you know, for …. For some reason other, other, Jewish names didn't do too well in entertainment. Eddie Cantor and Jack Benny and all those people changed their names. So I lived in…

984.t: First paid gig at thirteen with high school players
984.s: His first paid gig was a New Year's Eve at Wysocki's Restaurant with older high school musicians, whom he names.
984.q: My first gig, the first time I played for money I was 13 years old and we played at Wysocki’s Restaurant on New Year’s Eve in West Utica and it was a bunch of high school guys: Louie Angelini who I think is a professor of music at Utica College—

984.t: Weekends in Syracuse: The Embassy, Scott LaFaro and Pete Henderson
984.s: At 16 or 17 he goes to Syracuse to play at The Embassy with Scott LaFaro, Joe Close and Pete Henderson.
984.q: Well I started going to Syracuse when I was 16, 17, going on the weekends and I met people, guys who I’m sure you heard of, who are probably not familiar to anybody outside of that area, Sy Simpson the drummer — there was a club called The Embassy, right near where the Everson museum is now, maybe…

449.t: First paying gig with Teagarden and Hackett at eleven
449.s: Never worried about making a living; early TV work with Chubby Jackson led to a gig at eleven with Bobby Hackett and Jack Teagarden.
449.q: Never. Well since my whole family was musicians, the phone kind of started ringing after television. You know I didn’t have to go out and hustle up gigs. So I was fortunate in that way. No I never had any thought of that, I just followed my heart you know.

449.t: Atlantic City Jazz Festival at thirteen and playing without ambition
449.s: At thirteen he played the Atlantic City festival; he describes jamming weekly with older Black musicians with no thought of making it.
449.q: Before that, let me tell you, the next step after the Jack Teagarden/Bobby Hackett gig, my next big gig was when I was 13, the Atlantic City Jazz Festival. I was in a high school jazz band. I was only in grammar school or junior high and I was a lead trumpet and a jazz trumpet, and I went to this…

61.t: The Hot Jazz Classics reissue series begins
61.s: Offered $25 a week to research the catalog; the plant manager had his earlier letter; the plan was albums and singles.
61.ch: Hot Jazz Classics and how records were made
61.q: manager had said something like, “Yes, we had a letter from somebody suggesting some specific reissues that we ought to put out.” It turned out, when he pulled out the letter, that it was the letter that I had written several months before. I guess it was the early fall of 1939, or maybe even…

61.t: First byline: reviewing the Basie-Goodman Garden battle for Tempo
61.s: Stearns sent him to review the Madison Square Garden battle of the bands for Tempo.
61.ch: Yale, Stearns and the big bands
61.q: It’s a wonderful thrill. The great thing also about Marshall being there at that time was that as he got deeper into getting his Ph.d. in English literature, he wanted to stop doing so much writing. In the middle of my freshman year, Marshall was supposed to cover a Christmas week battle of the…

133.t: Dallas jam sessions with David Newman, Leroy Cooper and older players
133.s: As a younger teenager he was invited to jam with David Newman, Leroy Cooper, James Clay and Robert Moss, and played in a joint across from his home with his mother and grandmother Ruth and Louise's permission.
133.ch: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
133.q: Yeah, right around Dallas there was people like David Newman who we were in high school together and we would have jam sessions and I would be invited. I was a little younger than them, David and his generation. But I was invited because I was a Walton kid from down the street. [laughs] Give him a…

133.t: Dallas modern jazz underground; rhythm and blues on the bandstand
133.s: Walton says the rhythm was simplified for audiences and everything was rhythm and blues, but at fifteen or sixteen he was glad to be on any bandstand.
133.ch: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
133.q: No, the rhythm was uh, made simple, so to speak, you know, condescending in a way to the listeners. Well, in the sense to me when I think about it now. You know, I mean there just … we had to simplify. We can't play like we know it, that it could be very enjoyable here because people will start…

515.t: A week with Cab Calloway in Boston
515.s: At about 15 he played a week with Cab Calloway's show in his father's oversized tux.
515.q: Well, it was a week. It was a week gig in Boston. That was real early on. I was not yet a senior in high school. I might have been a junior...I might have been 15 years old, putting on a tux of my dad’s that was too big for me. Because I could read music, and I could play changes, so they hired…

515.t: Sitting in with his father's friends and the Four Sounds
515.s: Corea plays with older musicians, treats school as secondary, and has his first big gig with the Four Sounds.

134.t: First night at the Coconut Grove
134.s: The odd band of trumpet, drums and two saxes, a painted moustache, and four months until the club was raided.
134.ch: First job, society and reflections on time
