134.t: Fred the Cuban altoist hires him and his mother sets conditions
134.s: A neighbor drummer and altoist Fred offer a $2-a-night job; Freeman's mother questions Fred and makes him sign a promise.
134.ch: First job, society and reflections on time
134.q: They said even the nightclubs were, but I never saw any of it, really, because by that time I was working in nightclubs. I started in nightclubs when I was 12 years old, not in Chicago, but in Gary, Indiana. Some funny stories concerning all that too, because that was – everybody was wondering.…

491.t: First band job at the Wharton Settlement and being dropped by Mel Melvin
491.s: After four months he joined a small sextet for a $4 job at a settlement house, then joined the Mel Melvin band.
491.q: Things just accrued. After a while, I got good enough that I could play in a band. When I’d been playing about four months, somebody knocked on my door one day. It was a fellow. He says, “You Benny Golson?” I said, “Yeah.” He said, “I hear you play saxophone.” I said, “Yes.” A very quick “yes.” He…

491.t: Replaced in Jimmy Johnson's Ambassadors and his mother's advice
491.s: He and Coltrane rented tuxedos for little pay, then discovered the band was playing a cancelled gig without them; his mother consoled them.
491.q: We joined – John and I joined, and Ray Bryant, Jimmy Johnson and his Ambassadors. Being ambassadors, when you perform, you have to perform in a tuxedo. John and I didn’t have a tuxedo. So each time we worked, we had to rent a tuxedo. The tuxedo was $4 for the evening. Okay. The job paid 8. So for…

371.t: First band at thirteen in Pontiac and his father's rule about Saturday night
371.s: His first group with Jimmy Parker and others played local dances; he left the bandstand at midnight once when his father came for him.
371.ch: Early bands and the road to New York
371.q: Playing piano. I was working in a small group. We had a guitar player, a drummer, a tuba player who later played bass, and piano. We worked a little job in Pontiac. I did any number of little dances, where we had just kids. My brother, Thad, did some of the dances. A kid named James Murphy, and his…

371.t: Buffalo: the Anchor Bar trio without drums
371.s: A drumless trio with George Clark helped Jones develop his left hand.
371.ch: Early bands and the road to New York
371.q: It was very good. I worked with a tenor saxophonist named George Clock who had worked with Jimmy Lunceford at one time. Jimmy had a trio at The Anchor Bar. It was a fine Italian restaurant on Main Street in Buffalo. I guess it's still there on Main Street and North Street. Anyway, the trio…

16.t: Harlem Amateur Hour at the Apollo
16.s: He recalls winning $10 and a Poussepatuck Democratic Club date with a trio on Sweet Sue.
16.ch: City College, Juilliard and early bands
16.q: The Apollo Amateur Night, I think … see the Apollo Amateur Night had to happen during the time that I was in the Juilliard.

16.t: His first gigs: the Lunceford-style nine-piece band and Dizzy Gillespie
16.s: In high school he led a nine-piece band copying Lunceford; Dukie Divine failed to show at the St. Nicholas Palace and Dizzy Gillespie substituted. He graduated in 1935.
16.q: Well let me see. Oh, I'll tell you one notable one. When I was in high school, I decided that I was gonna copy everything that Jimmy Lunceford's band did. I loved Jimmy Lunceford's orchestra. I felt I needed a band to do it so I got 9 guys together and we had a nine-piece band and we tried to get…

651.t: Junior high and high school band and forming the Nighthawks
651.s: Disappointed that school band meant marching, he skipped band and formed the Nighthawks combo to play sock-hops and club dances.
651.q: Just a little bit. Just a little bit, yeah. When I went down to the junior high school downtown, I thought that’s where they were going to teach me everything about music. But I found out it was just kind of more like the sixth grade, only more people coming from the various elementary schools into…

651.t: Sitting in at Louisville clubs as a teenager
651.s: At 16 he drove to Louisville black clubs such as the Diamond Horseshoe, heard Fort Knox players, and sat in on sax.
651.q: Not really. Not that I can think of. I think at the end of each school day, I couldn’t wait to get out. I was pretty narrow-vision, I guess. Music—and that was about it. When you get to 16, you want to get some sort of a car, and at that stage I could go to Louisville. I found clubs

108.t: Jimmy Gorham's band while still in school
108.s: Deciding music might be a living, he plays in Jimmy Gorham's band imitating the big bands, where older players tease him as Junior.
108.ch: Childhood and learning music in Philadelphia
108.q: I didn’t really know whether I – music in Philadelphia was a little – it was a very difficult profession at that time, because there was no great volume of work, certainly not for most of the black musicians. My father was a pretty busy musician. So by those standards, they were kept pretty active.…

108.t: Early Philadelphia bands: King Coleman, Sadler, Gorham, Harlem Dictators, Slappy
108.s: After school he plays with several local groups, ending with Lonnie Slappy's small band where he developed his improvising.
108.ch: Childhood and learning music in Philadelphia
108.q: I started playing with – I got a call to go out. I played with several bands in Philadelphia at the same time I was in school. I played with Jimmy Gorham’s band. The first band, oddly enough – I played with a man called King Coleman. He was a friend of my father’s. He was a pianist. He had a little…

508.t: Gigs and money with The Creators
508.s: Clubs, fraternities and weddings paid more than his father's jazz gigs, so he learned the songs to keep working.
508.q: Night clubs, fraternities, dances, proms, weddings. You name it, we were doing it. So we were working a lot. 508.t: The Creators: his role in the band and moving from keyboards to saxophone
508.s: The band's original members and why he left the heavy Fender Rhodes for alto saxophone.

953.t: First professional gig around age thirteen and his mother waiting up
953.s: He recounts his first job in the Bronx at about thirteen, with older players doing popular songs without arrangements, and his mother waiting for him.
953.ch: Music in Harlem: records, radio, gigs
953.q: Well, Larry, here’s what happened. I was...I recounted this recently, because they did a story last year about, um, uh in The Wall Street Journal. This guy took me back uptown to where I lived. I don’t know if you saw that. Anyway, I was about uh well...I don’t know, I was around 13 or something…

953.t: Paying his way: working from age eleven
953.s: He answers about money for shows by saying he began working at eleven delivering clothes.
953.ch: Music in Harlem: records, radio, gigs
953.q: Well, I, uh...I started working when I was eleven years old. When I came out of school, I got a job uh delivering clothes from the cleaners, tailors. I used to do, do, do that when I was eleven. I’m very proud of that, because my wife would try to say, “Oh, you didn’t start–,” I’d say, “Well, when…

367.t: Carter band sidemen and his age when he joined
367.s: Young names Tizo Miller, Eddie Berg and Tweedlin' Beard and says he was fifteen or sixteen when he joined.
367.q: Chick Carter‘s band, there was a lot of good guys in that band, came out of that band. Tizo Miller. Curtis Miller, he went with somebody else, Tizo. Eddie Berg on drums. You just remind of Eddie, something about you reminds me of Eddie Berg. He had a great smile, a great everything, but he could…

367.t: Playing small clubs for about twenty dollars
367.s: Young recalls playing steadily in little clubs for eighteen to twenty dollars and bands that never reached the big time.
367.q: You see, we played consistently in Chick Carter‘s band because in them days there was all kind of little clubs that the bands would play in and the band was playing, we wasn‘t making nothing. You‘d make eighteen or nineteen, twenty dollars at the most. That‘s very good if you got that. But the…

109.t: The Guy Lombardo-style band in Cincinnati
109.s: He and Cobbs joined a Black band that copied Guy Lombardo exactly, hired by a club owner, to save money for college.
109.q: So we began to make gigs. So I ran into a saxophone player who played like Guy Lombardo. His whole band played like Guy Lombardo. Now, will you imagine that. And he asked Cal and I to join his band. Now we played

109.t: Subbing for Biddie Johnson with saxophonist Gene Jenkins
109.s: Drummer Biddie Johnson asked him to cover his club job; with a trio and Gene Jenkins' help he learned to play for dancers and word spread about the new young drummer.
109.ch: Learning drums and Roy Eldridge's band
109.q: And he says, 'Do you think you could hold the job down? I'll just be gone a couple of weeks.' So I said, 'Listen, Biddie, I'm afraid --,' He said, 'Oh, think nothing of it. I'll be here a couple of days and you come every night and I'll show you just how it goes.

230.t: Golden Pheasant job, skipping school, and one-nighters

230.q: Well, I got jobs around in some of the -- oh, I worked at a Chinese-American restaurant on 23rd Street, while I was still going to school, called the Golden Pheasant. And what I'd do is I'd -- I was going to a school called Berkeley-Irving on West 83rd Street, and I'd come in and I'd answer the…

230.t: First band as Fred Black and the S.S. Republic ship job
230.s: His first band, non-union and under the name Fred Black, played four days at a Broadway Chinese-American restaurant; in summer 1929 he got the ship's orchestra job on the Republic.
230.q: Well, actually the first band I had was quite a large band for that particular time, and it also happened to have been a non-union band. There was a restaurant on Broadway, upstairs, a Chinese-American restaurant, at the corner of 50th, where -- yes, 50th Street and Broadway, and they had gotten…

88.t: Child labor law ends his club job; the dancer Jack Williams
88.s: The Labor Commission stopped Lee and the dancer Jack Williams working at the club, after which Lee turned seriously to music.

88.q: So I was in school, and I met a guy that was going to Jefferson High School, and I was going to Lafayette Junior High School, and so because he was a real good dancer, and we had an assembly at Lafayette, and he came over from Jeff and he and I did a number together, you know? And I told Curtis…

88.t: Filling in for married drummers at five black bands
88.s: Lee worked free on nights off for drummers in five bands at Long Beach and elsewhere to gain experience before the Papa Mutt job.
88.ch: Early Los Angeles and first bands
88.q: on playing whatever the job called for, you know, and I'll tell you a funny story of what I did when I got started in L.A.

409.t: Joining Eagle Eye Shields in Jacksonville
409.s: Edmond Hall went to pianist-leader Eagle Eye Shields, recommended Cootie, and his father arranged for his Jacksonville partner to look after him.
409.ch: First bands and the road in the South
409.q: They played by ear. They didn't have no music. And Edmund Hall left the Pensacola Jazz Band, and he went to Florida to join another band by the name of Eagle Eye Shields.

409.t: Sitting in with the Pensacola Jazz Band and Edmond Hall
409.s: At about sixteen he sat in with Edmond Hall in the Pensacola Jazz Band, a Dixieland group playing by ear, when they visited Mobile.
409.ch: First bands and the road in the South
409.q: So Edmund Hall Hogg was playing with the Pensacola Jazz Band, and they came to Mobile, and I sat in with them and played. And that's how I got started out.

167.t: Playing parties and social functions as a small boy
167.s: He played dances and Saturday-night social functions alone, his father dropping him off and fetching him at midnight, earning about $13-14.
167.q: And then I'd get hired to play the little -- what do you call them now? I forget now what you call them. What do you call them things, now? See, that's been so long....

167.t: First club date and his own group at eleven
167.s: His first club dates, around Long Island, came about 1925 with his own group when he was a child, his parents taking him to the jobs.
167.q: Yes. And I took my own little group, and my mother would take me and leave me, and my father would come back and get me. And after that, I made about $7.00 or $8.00.

70.t: Buckeye Melodians and drummer Gerald Hobson
70.s: His first band was the Buckeye Melodians at home; later Earl Warren's father took it over, and Gerald Hobson encouraged him with stories of New York.
70.ch: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
70.q: Later on Earl Warren, you know, the saxophone player, his father later took it over after I left home. And Earl was just starting to play at that time, just starting to learn to play saxophone.

70.t: Wesley Helvey's phone call and leaving Springfield
70.s: Helvey, hearing of him through Hobson, calls the undertaker's office and hires him; Jackson makes sure the Brick crowd sees him leave town.
70.ch: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
70.q: And I was singing, too, so he told me, he said, "You know, Quentin," he said, "you got a good chance to make it in music." He said, "I'm going to Cincinnati and if I see anybody out there that wants a trombone player, I'll tell him about you because I think you got a good chance." So he went to…

452.t: First summer tour with Frank Davis and the Harlem Grill with Chester Boone
452.s: At sixteen Cobb tours Louisiana with Frank Davis, then joins Chester Boone's band at the Harlem Grill for $34 a week while his mother earned $10; the dates are sorted out along the way.
452.ch: First bands, illness and Houston life
452.q: a guy from Louisiana by the name of Frank Davis, and this was in 1934 during the summer month when school was out. And, of course, I was the youngest guy in the group, at my age, and I have to think what age I was then, because you're turning me down; you can figure it by years if I was born in…

452.t: Russell and Illinois Jacquet start out as a dance team
452.s: The Jacquet brothers began in Houston as dancers, and Cobb recalls root beer jobs paying 75 cents.
452.q: started out in Houston as a dance team; neither one of them could blow a horn. They danced. They had a dance team. We used to play root beer jobs on a platform where people would come in and buy root beer, you know, and we'd get 75¢ a night, and then people would throw money up on the -- for tips.

233.t: Cy begs again and Monk accepts
233.s: Cy insisted he could fake it, called back begging, and Monk, curious and sweating, agreed.
233.q: Anyhow, he was just insistent. 'Well, that's OK. You can cut it. I know you can handle it. You're a natural.' I was just...He was giving me the kind of razzmatazz that it was just natural for me to play the bass, to play music, that it was in my family.

233.t: Cy Jones phones the foundry asking for a bassist
233.s: Honking tenor player Cy Jones phoned Monk at the foundry for a Friday and Saturday after-hours job; Monk refused, not ready.
233.q: Now, the word had got out that I had a bass. All right. And there was a guy there by the name of Cy Jones, was a tenor player. And Cy Jones, he wasn't a tenor player's tenor player by no means.

71.t: First jazz gig at five dollars with four songs
71.s: A visiting five-piece band hired Clayton after only a few months on trumpet; he knew four tunes and played them all night.
71.q: Jazz? Well I started in Parsons. But one time there was a band that came to my home that their trumpet player had got sick on the way there and he couldn't play. It was only about a five-piece band. And they had to play this dance. And they would have given anything to find a trumpet player. And…

71.t: A band at age eight with piano, drums and combs
71.s: He recalls leading a little party band as a child pianist and the pay of a few dollars each.
71.q: Oh yes, yes. I had a band when, oh way before that. I had a band when I was about eight years old which was me playing piano, and I had a drummer and two little guys played tissue with a comb. And we used to, we used to play for parties. Give us two or three dollars a piece. Because I could play…

29.t: Playing dances with his brother Dean
29.s: At about fifteen he and drummer brother Dean played all the local dances for two or three dollars a night.
29.q: Round about -- I was about, let me see if I can get my age straightened out. I was just a little kid running around the streets.

29.t: Wood Wilson's band, his first professional work
29.s: Howard says his first professional work was with Wood Wilson's small band, not the Syncopators, playing tenor.
29.q: I don't know what they called that boy, just called him Wood Wilson's Band.

418.t: First gigs, the wish to be a comedian, and playing by ear at 17
418.s: He earned about 50 cents at his first gig, once wanted to be a comedian, and at 17 played by ear using only the tonic note.
418.q: Well, I didn't make any money, you know, just... At the first gig I ever made, I think I made 50 cents or something. But I kind of liked it, you know. I liked that. Of course, in retrospect(?)... I wanted to be a comedian, too. That was another ambition I had.

418.t: The union job for a reading trombonist and buying a used trombone
418.s: The Columbus union sent him to a band wanting a trombonist who could read; he bluffed, paid a bandmate fifteen dollars a week for a trombone, and was fired after a month.
418.q: So all I wanted to know was the tonic, you know, and then I would go from there. I used to like to sing in quartets and things, so I could always play the second... I could always play the second or third chorus just by hearing it.

99.t: First jobs with Toe Morgan, Christmas 1924, and the stolen watch
99.s: Drummer 'Toe' Morgan brings him to a $5 Christmas matinee dance; at a Fairman's job he is robbed of his watch on the ride home.
99.q: So, I went on back and went back to the woodshed, as we called it. Went back to the woodshed and kept on practicing, kept on practicing. So, I got so I could play a few tunes. 170.t: First real bass, a Big Bill Broonzy blues record date, and drums after hours

170.q: But that's when I got my first, real bass violin. I was still going to school, high school, junior high, and Buster got a record date for me. I'll never forget this. And I had to get permission from my teacher to make it, although I'm working every night. We worked from, say, about 9 or 10 o' clock…

170.t: Playing the fiddle with Buster Bennett at the Tuxedo Inn
170.s: Mr. Robinson buys Ware a fiddle for his club band with Buster Bennett and Martha Davis; he is paid little and repays the instrument.
170.q: I was in school, and I don't know -- they knew that a few of us in the school was playing around, you know; we had a piano player, Horace Parnum, and I took my fiddle to school one day for assembly, and we played. That was just before I got out of grade school to go to Wendell Phillips. I would…

19.t: Drummer Leo Gilpoopy hires him for the Atlantic Beer Garden
19.s: Just before sixteen he is recruited to play duo seven nights a week at twelve dollars a week.
19.ch: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
19.q: So I guess it was just before my sixteenth birthday... I was standing in front of my house one day, with some of the other guys who I was playing around with. 19.t: Substituting for his teacher at a club on E Street
19.s: Aged fifteen he fills in for an hour with saxophonist Winbush and drummer Eugene Carroll, his first professional-feeling job.
19.ch: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
19.q: So before long, to make a long story short, being a professional musician himself, he was playing at a little I guess you'd call it club down on E Street between 10th and 11th Street. 74.t: Playing with Ethel Waters in Little Rock
74.s: While still in high school he and Swazey augment Ethel Waters's small band for two days, one of his first professional jobs.
74.ch: Trent's band: touring, sidemen and breakup
74.q: I forgot the name of the band, but she didn't have enough--she wanted to augment it, so Swazey and I augmented the band.

74.t: Meeting Trent through Eugene Cook and a summer drug store job
74.s: Cook hears his swing solo at a parade and hires him; the band plays for tips outside a drug store in Arkansas until his mother sends the police.
74.ch: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
74.q: With him. Cook heard me play. We did a parade out at sweet home and somebody pointed this guy out to me. 149.t: First professional job at Jones Beach
149.s: The band's first professional engagement was a week at a Jones Beach restaurant in about 1932.
149.ch: Forming the band in New York
149.q: No. You know, while we was in school, I just thought about this. We came up special to play a week at Jones Beach in one of the restaurants there. We played a week there. I think that was 1932. We played that week and went back to school.

149.t: Jobbing with George Uge at Tuxedo Park and school music
149.s: As a boy he played parties, dances and a summer at Tuxedo Junction with drummer George Uge, and in school played military music and french horn.
149.q: Well, there (inaudible) used to be a band leader there. I can't recall his name right now. It may come to me later. He used to play out the "Tuxedo Junction". George Uge was the name.

30.t: First kids' band playing 'The Sheik' for gate money
30.s: He left for Chicago at 18; before that he and boyhood friends such as Landry learned together, knew three tunes including 'The Sheik', and played yard parties for a quarter apiece.
30.q: Oh, I played with several bands. In fact, when I first started out we had a couple of fellows (instruments) that was learning -- one, by the name of Landry, was trying to play trumpet, and we had another guy trying to play drums. And it was all youngsters and we were all learning together at the

30.t: Follow-up: Landry, the three-tune band, and Gaspard's name
30.s: Henry Landry was the trumpeter in the kids' band that played two sheiks and the blues for gate receipts; Bigard cannot yet recall Gaspard's full name.
30.q: Yeah. We were all kids together, just fooling around. And we used to -- every Saturday night we'd go find out who was giving a party or something and we'd play for the gate receipt. 389.t: High school orchestra and playing five nights a week
389.s: He joined the high school orchestra, played dances five nights a week and summers at Harvey's Lake.
389.q: the high school orchestra and that was a -- there were several who played jobs. guys there, several musicians there, A drummer who played quite a bit around, a piano player who played around quite a bit and we had another saxophone player there, a trumpet player.

389.t: The Scranton Sirens offers and the Dorseys
389.s: He turned down the Scranton Sirens twice, after sitting in with Freddie Small and leader Billy Lustig, and recalls hearing the Dorseys there.
389.q: So the Mason Dixon -- then I heard the Scranton Sirens and although I had heard about the Dorsey Brothers, because they were from I think Laneeford, not far away in the coal regions, but I had made up my mind, I had an offer from the Scranton Sirens.

75.t: Splicky's washboard band and the union
75.s: At about 13 he did a few jobs with a washboard band led by a man known only as Splicky, around the Alhambra stage acts and the union rules.
75.q: : No, I wasn't in the union yet. But I did a couple of things with Splicky's(?) band, a washboard band, you know -- a couple in Harlem. They were turning around ...(?)... And the union said... By that time the Alhambra had acts, and you were supposed to go on the stage. But when it came time to…

75.t: Why he became a musician; piano battles in Harlem studios
75.s: Piano beat grocery and tailor jobs as a livelihood; he describes the Cave and Jack and Jill studios, piano battles, and social-club work at Dunbar and the Renaissance.
75.ch: Teens, stride pianists and the Louisiana Stompers
75.q: You asked me what made me go into playing piano, to be a musician. It was better than working in a grocery store, or delivering suits at a tailor, a place... Like, we had the Spotless Cleaners and the Burger Service and things like that, you know. I done that also. Then I found that it was more to…

97.t: Weekend jobs with Honey Potter's band on Long Island
97.s: Saxophonist Cecil Smith brings Scott, still in high school, to Honey Potter's band for firemen's and policemen's balls.
97.q: Well, it so happened that in playing around, I met one of the fellows that was in the band, by the name of Cecil Smith. He was a saxophone player. He became interested in me, I don't know why. He just liked me, that's all. And talking with fellows I'd met, musicians. And he asked me, hey, Scotty,…

97.t: Neighborhood boys bands, block parties and High School of Commerce bands
97.s: He moves uptown, joins the Dover brothers' band, plays block parties and dances, and plays in school bands.
97.q: Well, that was downtown. We slowly moved uptown. This is Manhattten, and I became acquainted with some older fellows, and a boys band was two young fellows. Willie and Lewis Dover, had a band. And I heard of it, and they had heard of me. So we got together. It was a nice little band, young fellows,…

76.t: Marge's nurse training and her brother putting her in the band
76.s: Marge quit nurse training after a quarrel with a supervisor, so her brother Charlie made her play piano in his dance band, starting at the Almac dance hall.
76.ch: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
76.q: So when I finished high school I wasn't doing anything, and my sister was going to college. I didn't want to go to college, I didn't want to be a school teacher or anything like that, and it was so hard on my mother sending my sister to college, I didn't want nobody to work that hard for me. And so…

76.t: The six-piece band and the name Jazz-O-Maniacs
76.s: At 19 Marge played in Charlie's six-piece band; as jazz came in he named it Charlie Creath and his Jazz-O-Maniacs.
76.ch: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
76.q: 18, 19, because I had been out of high school. Still not 20 because I'd been out of high school hanging around there, didn't know what I wanted to do. But I didn't want to go to college, I know that. I didn't want -- not that I didn't love school and all, but my mother had to work too hard. So my…

77.t: Begging cabarets for work and learning songs from a player piano
77.s: She sneaked out nightly asking clubs to hire her, finally got a chance at Dago Frank's, learned songs from a player piano, and stayed a year and ten months until the police closed it.
77.q: Gave me the job peeling potatoes. And so, I peeled the potatoes and stayed there, and in the meantime, I used to -- when I was -- I would sit there and hear them say that girls made $10.00 a week in nightclubs. They didn't call them nightclubs. What did they call them then? I don't know what they…

77.t: Asking cabarets for work and starting at Dago Frank's
77.s: After the boarding house closes she asks cabarets to hire her, is finally taken on at Dago Frank's by Roy and the pianist Bruce for $10 a week; her first nightclub job.
77.q: So when the lady closed the boarding house, during that time I was working for her I was going to the different places called -- didn't call them nightclubs, because that was too modern. I don't know what they called them. But anyhow, I would go to each one and ask them -- the way I approached them…

455.t: Miss Puckett chaperones the boys' band on tours
455.s: A hip neighborhood lady books the child band into small Texas towns and settles pay back home with home brew and deductions.
455.q: Yeah, it may come to me a little later on, but anyway, we had been getting together and rehearsing, and we had a pretty good little old band. We used to just sit around in each other's back yards and play, and whatnot, and so a lady by the name of Miss Puckett, she heard us, and she

455.t: Ernest Williams offers a Tulsa roadhouse job
455.s: Southern Serenaders drummer Ernest Williams books the boys into a Tulsa road house; Budd explains road houses and his earlier Dallas job with Red Calhoun.
455.q: So anyway, we -- there was a band called the Southern Serenaders, from Tulsa, Oklahoma, and they had a drummer. His name was Ernest Williams. Ernest was a sharp little dude. He reminded me a lot of J. C. ~~Herd~~ Heard. You know, he was about that size, and he was just --

529.t: First bass job and the first $50 pay envelope
529.s: Older men in a Central Avenue club hire him; he knows few standards but gets by on blues, and is stunned by $50 pay, more than his uncle earned.
529.q: Count Basie's and--and then one thing led to another. There was a--there was a quintet playing in a club right on the corner of Central and Scott. And uh, I guess these people saw me carrying this bass and they--

529.t: Brass Rail trio in Tampa and local resentment
529.s: With Ralph Dewey, Johnny Burdine and a drummer he works the Brass Rail for $125 a week, and local men resent the young stars.
529.q: So, one thing led on to another, and then I--the Brass Rail. I started meeting guys, ....younger musician. And there was another grown man. His name was Ralph Dewey. So he got me to play the bass and another friend of mine to play the drums and a saxophone player named Johnny Burdine. All of us was…

98.t: Stomp King's hustling band in the roadhouses
98.s: He left high school to join Stomp King, who found cars and roadhouses outside Chicago, passed the hat, and moved on; it was Saunders's first working band.
98.ch: Childhood, first drums and the hustling years
98.q: No, I lost track of a lot of them, because I didn't go all the way through high school. I left, and then I went travelling, I travelled an awful lot. First, before that I joined a guy around here called Stump King. And all the musicians -- see, in those days, things were really rough, they were…

98.t: Playing a full drum set in Stomp King's fake band
98.s: He moved to a full drum set while hustling, before sock cymbals existed; the band was three to six pieces playing tunes of the day, with top musicians sitting in for four or five dollars.
98.ch: Childhood, first drums and the hustling years
98.q: Oh, I started then after I come out, and we started to go into hustling and things like this, then I started on the set of drums. There was no such thing as a sock cymbal back there, then.

13.t: First professional job with Monroe Richardson's band at Midway Gardens
13.s: A friend, later his brother-in-law, recommends him to a nine-piece band; they play weekends opposite Art Kassel at Midway Gardens.
13.q: Well, there's one reason why I didn't finish school. A friend of mine heard me on tuba, and he recommended me to a band leader that had a orchestra.

13.t: Art Simms's band in Milwaukee, Bernie Young and commuting from school
13.s: He plays Riverside Gardens in Milwaukee with Art Simms, with Preston Jackson, picked up at school; Bernie Young takes over after Simms dies.
13.q: Still going to school. And then that same band was taken over by Art Simms. He played violin and we got a job up in Milwaukee. Three nights a week.

242.t: First jobs and playing with older men like Gassum
242.s: He cannot recall his first job but played with older men, including a banjoist Gassum's band at 12 or 13.
242.q: No, my very first job. I never thought about that. My first job. Where was my first job? You know, I can't think about my really first job. What band might be with the kids that played with you? At that time, no, when I was playing, I used to play with older men. I was playing that good.

174.t: Going on the riverboat with Sun White and playing for the roustabouts
174.s: Through friend Luis Andre he joined a riverboat band, washing dishes and playing excursions; he played blues on clarinet for roustabouts, and was hired at the Japanese Tea Garden because he could read.
174.q: That must have been around maybe 23, 24, maybe 21, I don't know. I was a youngster, I know, because I tell you, we didn't have nothing to do in the day at all. Sun White was washing dishes in the kitchen, and playing with the band at night. And I would be so tired, I was a youngster, just out of,…

177.t: First bands, first lawn-party job, and sitting in with Chris Kelly
177.s: A band with Lawrence Randall was too timid to play; he formed one with Lawrence Toker, played a lawn party for two and a half dollars, then sat in with Chris Kelly and got hired.
177.q: Well, after I got the drum, as I told you, my uncle got the drum from a forum shop. I was going to Lansing. I had a fellow come to bring society notice to my house. His name was Lawrence Randall. He said, I told him I had a drum. He said, well, I got a trumpet. I'm learning how to play music. He…

864.t: First brass band job with Old Man Allen and his Navy years
864.s: His first brass band job was with Old Man Allen; he left the Navy in 1919 and began playing in 1922.
864.ch: Tulane, Tuxedo and Waifs' Home bands
864.q: I didn't play with any of them. Uh, Old Man Allen? What about him? Oh, you know I played with him. Yeah. He had one of my first bands.

244.t: Getting hired by Sidney Desvigne for the Steamer Capital
244.s: Alfred Williams recommended him; after one rehearsal Desvigne hired him.
244.q: Well, I was recommended by the same guy Alfred Williams which was very instrumental in my welfare and so he recommended me to Sidney Desmond he says I have a How do you spell Sidney's name? S-I-D-N-E-Y D-I-S-V-I-G-N-E Uh-huh. And I played with him I mean I was Alfred introduced me to Sidney Desmond…

246.t: First music job with the stave handlers' band
246.s: Glass played his first job for the stave handlers' parade band with Walter Blue and Edward Gaspar.
246.q: Really? Yeah, that's the time Walter Blue dropped dead. They call themselves the stave handlers. They used to handle, they call them now car unloaders. They unload them cars out on the other side of Jackson Avenue up in there. Handling staves for the make bows. They call themselves the stave…

178.t: First bands: Starlight Serenade and house parties
178.s: He recalls his first band, its members, the two trumpets, playing house parties for small pay, and moving on to better outfits.
178.q: I can't quite remember who was in that band. What kind of band was it? It was a little five or six piece of music. Did you play for music? I used to play off little choruses written down.

253.t: First job with the Thomas band in Reserve
253.s: Hall recalls his first band, a group of kids around Reserve, and struggles to name the drummer, bassist and trombonist.
253.q: My very first job, I think it was with Thomas Band, it's been so long ago, I think it was Thomas, just a bunch of kids, we picked up our instruments after playing.

182.t: Sox's Lane: starting out with Eddie Vincent and a four-piece band
182.s: Tom recalls Sox's Lane as where he began playing, forming a four-piece band with Eddie Vincent, Skeeter and Jolie on bass.
182.q: With Freddie Kepler. That's right. Mm-hmm. Well, I was the one who pitched him. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Me and him just started together in Sox's Lane. Mm-hmm. That's been years ago. Mm-hmm. And then we made up a band with Skeeter. Like you see, it was Skeeter and different fellas. And I coached him playing…

899.t: First job at house parties and brother's Original Cloverleaf
899.s: The first job was a house party for Italian people; he later played a long time in his brother's Original Cloverleaf orchestra.
899.q: No, just around town, different little house parties, you know. This was for some Italian people we played that night. I always think about my first job.

826.t: Black Pete, Cock-Eye George and the first paid job
826.s: Reminiscence of Black Pete and Cock-Eye George, who took Willie on his first paid job, then playing at George Delcy's place.
826.q: Yeah, well that's my first job. He took me on. I was playing the violin. And he took me on a job for the butcher where he used to buy meat. Pete in the Padres Market. You knew Pete. Sure. Well we played for him. He lived around Scott and Canal.

183.t: The Unholy Three in a Johnson Street speakeasy
183.s: Playing cornet in a three-piece band at two dollars a night, Watts kept a promise to his mother not to drink or smoke until he was 25, and tells of the speakeasy's paymaster.
183.ch: Learning trumpet and first bands in New Orleans
183.q: Well, he was playing drums. This man's going to give us two dollars a night in this joint, three pieces. Had old beat-up piano back in the corner, one of them old uprights, you know. And Lang would sit on my right side. I'd sit on top the old upright, take the front out, and I'd sit on top, just…

891.t: Starting out following Chris Kelly's band around 1923
891.s: Colar says he began by following Chris Kelly's band and others as a kid; at about 18 he lived near Marigny and Rampart and recalls trains to the Exclusion baptisms.
891.q: started out following Chris Kelly's band, Wooden Jewels, Lions Band, Cuckoo, Buddy Petit, points of, I was a kid, but actually I mean played with during that time like followed Chris Kelly, set and played with him, Wooden Jewels,

725.t: Gigging with Buddy Petit around Covington and Mississippi
725.s: He played banjo around 1918 with Buddy Petit's rough gig band in small towns, then in one-night aggregations.
725.q: Yeah, back in the day, as far as I can remember, I played with Bonnie Bigard and myself. Little Scram band, Buddy PT, you know, back in the... That band wasn't rated with these bands like this. I mean, they played... Just gig around, you know. Lot of colored work. For the white people, they played…

1000.t: First job at Ben Mulligan's saloon with Manuel Manetta
1000.s: His first job was at Judge Ben Mulligan's saloon on Rampart with George Jones, with Manetta playing piano.
1000.q: That was Judge LeBlanc. And I think he had no legs on the last, after a while I heard he had lost his legs. He's dead now, I know.

262.t: McNeil's first job and bands since
262.s: The Patterson Hotel job with John Patterson, local outfits, Hal Kristoff and the old-timers he has played with.
262.q: Well my first job is professional so you sort of speak is the way you get some money for it. We had a little outfit we broke off and organized on our own. And they was mostly I think we played for the Patterson's and we had one of the fellas who was a little more advanced. He's one of the greats…

957.t: First drums and the Ivy Theater trio at age eight
957.s: At eight he played at the Ivy Theater with a white clarinetist and pianist, sitting on a special stool and hidden on the balcony because he was so small.
957.q: My first set of drums, Maggie Garnier. There you saw in the Ivy Theater, Annette and Villery. Well, I used to throw out circles for her. I also played there with a white band. It was three pieces. Two white fellas and myself. Piano, clarinet, and drum.

762.t: Brother's rehearsals and his first paid job
762.s: His brother's band rehearsed at home; Purnell got his first job as a singer and two-piece pianist during the depression and was paid fifteen dollars.
762.q: Yeah. My brother at that time had begun to take up the saxophone and we were living together. And oh they used to have ten and fifteen fellas every day used to rehearse them back there. They rehearsed them so much that I knew a number from the introduction to the corner stop. I could whistle it, I…

37.t: First professional job in 1949 and meeting Marty Grosz
37.s: Chace's first job was on April 2, 1949, with John Holmgren's band, the day his father died; he then describes the young Chicago players around Marty, including Don Ewell and Bob Lovett.
37.q: i don't know i was gonna play let's see if you want to document this this is april 2nd 1949 i was about to have my first professional engagement with john holmgren leading the band out on uh... dempster in skokie on dempster street just west of mccormick shut and he hired he hired floyd bean and…

264.t: First job: the Merit band and two dollars at a house party
264.s: Zardis's first paid job at age 19 or 20 with the Merit band, his mother's skepticism, and the next Saturday's dance on Frenchman Street.
264.q: Maybe. Well he was no big man, but he could read pretty much. And we had another fellow who was playing the trombone, but he was playing a vowel trombone, his name was Charlie, we called him Big Charlie, big tall man, we had about, oh man, he was about seven foot tall, eight foot tall. And he had…

266.t: First gig at a block party and early pay
266.s: His first paid job was a neighborhood block party for about $25 a band, with a six to eight piece group, later $35 gigs with singer Teresa Kelly.
266.q: And she hired the band to play this block party, which would be, I'm trying to think of which side is which. On Knaustra, you know where the Warren Easton side is. I'm trying to think of the block party. I'm trying to think of the block party. I'm trying to think of the neighborhood. Ah, jeez I'm…

620.t: First jobs: Cronlite Walk and Lucian's Pavilion at the lake
620.s: His first jobs were house parties, a place on Cronlite Walk (Lafitte Street) and Lucian's Pavilion on the lake at about 17, always playing solo.
620.ch: First jobs and the piano scene
620.q: Oh, I played in house parties around. I played at a place called Old Mill Street. It was on Cronlite Walk between Broad and White. I played there. I remember that being about one of the first jobs I was playing piano back there.

40.s: His first band was a four-piece group in Metairie in 1949; it broke up and he put the horn away until joining the Straws.
40.q: Well, I think the first actual band that I ever played with was about nineteen, nineteen forty-nine. We had a four-piece group out in Metry. And well over a period of years, some of the boys got married, some went in the service, and we just dispersed. And I've been lucky enough to run up on…

817.t: First bands: the family trio and Classy's band
817.s: His first band was a trio with his saxophone-playing brother for house parties, paid at ten or eleven; he first played string bass in Classy's band.
817.q: Well, the first one that I remember was a little group that we had. My second brother was a saxophone player at the time, and we had a little trio. We had a, I played the drum at the time, my brother played the saxophone, and we had a boy with a banjo. He later went over the piano and we got…

271.t: First professional job at the Green Roof Social Club
271.s: His first paid job was $2 for four hours at the Green Roof Social Club with Weimanson's band, around 1903.
271.ch: Early string bands and first jobs
271.q: We played for the Green Roof Social Club, Marais and Bethania. William Schenk was there. He was the proprietor of the saloon and the Green Roof, too. That was the first job I ever played. With a magnificent sum of $2, four hours. That wasn't bad for those days. No, it was pretty good. Next.

272.t: Tom's Roadhouse as first job after service; pickup hiring
272.s: First job after the service came from fellows who heard him; no contracts, the same men played everywhere, and he stayed only a couple of weeks.
272.ch: Back from service and early jobs
272.q: Well, Tom's Roadhouse is the way I got the job, the first job I got after the service, you know, when I came back from the service. Well, then I went there and, well, a couple of fellas saw me and asked me, I told him, so, so, and so, you know what I mean? Just nothing. I just got in town, come on,…

818.s: Coquille's first job was with Joseph Salvaggio's Lombardo-type kid band; they rehearsed hard, played West End roof jobs, and he left after about three years for the Blue Parody hoping to reach the Streeman band.
818.q: No, but we had a boy that played the bass horn, like Lombardo has. And after four hour rehearsals two or three times a week, one year later, it really sounded great. We really, then we began getting jobs on a West End roof, and spot jobs. We all had things to do in a day, so we couldn't take steady…

799.t: First jobs with Ernest Stevens: park concerts and picnics
799.s: His first job was with barber-bandleader Ernest Stevens, playing marches in parks in a big band where he faked his way at about seventeen.
799.q: Oh the first job I played with a fellow by the name of Stevens, Ernest Stevens, who was from way downtown on St. Claude Street. He was a barber. And on the side he made up little concert groups. And we used to go in the parks and play concerts. That's when I was, oh gee this was so long ago. And…

45.t: First job with the Columbia Band at Butcher Hill, age 16
45.s: At sixteen Williams played his first job with the Columbia Band, naming its members including Tick Chambers, Ernest Kelly and Roy Palmer.
45.q: When I started playing, when I played my first job, I was 16. I played with the Columbia Band up on Oak and Protection Levy at a place, a dance hall called Butcher Hill.

278.t: Business versus music and the RCA album
278.s: He entered business out of necessity; he recounts how Danny Kessler heard him playing behind others and recorded his first album for RCA.
278.q: Oh yes. All the time. All the time. Right. I, I entered the business part just out of necessity. No love for the business at all. I understand it. I don't dislike it. I have a lot of respect for it and I believe that this business is, is as legit as any business around in any country. And I think…

12.t: Career summary from lessons to the Oliver band and Shanghai
12.s: Nicholas recounts lessons with Wooden Joe and the Tios, early bands, the Navy, his own group, King Oliver in Chicago, Shanghai and the trip home.
12.q: Well, I started taking lessons around 9 years of age with my uncle, Wooden Joe Nicholas. He was my big influence on this jazz scene. And later on, I went to Papa Teo and took lessons with him for about a couple of years. Then Lorenzo Teo, his son. And finished up with him until around 1915. Then I…

475.t: First job in Marrero and early bands
475.s: His first job was across the river in Marrero with Peter Hicks, then bands with cousins and Earl Vinnett in St. Rose before returning to New Orleans.
475.q: The first job I had was across the river. And I played over in Marrero. And during those times I think I made four hours I believe, first job. Well that was plenty of money then. That was pretty good for those days. Yeah. Yeah. Plenty of money in those days. And I played with a band, it was Peter…

724.t: First band job at Artesian Hall with the Morgans
724.s: He is sent to substitute at Artesian Hall for the Morgan band, his first band job; the Morgans were mostly ear players.
724.q: Well, the first job I played with a band. I, Zeldon Morgan, was playing over at the Artesian Hall one night and the client up there, Adolfo was playing over at the Artesian Hall one night and the first one night was playing with him. For some reason he couldn't so he asked me to go over there. He…

189.t: Becoming professional: summers in Alexandria and early wages
189.s: Led his own band at 15 playing a black hotel in Alexandria at fifteen dollars a week; cost of groceries.
189.q: Oh in Alexandria we played at a hotel, a black hotel. They had upstairs at the hotel and downstairs there was a dance hall and like a club. And we used to play there every night. We were staying at the hotel upstairs, downstairs. We'd go down and play every night. In other words I thought that was…

281.t: First jobs with Brunis, Schoebel and Snyder at Blatt's Palm Gardens
281.s: One of his first jobs was with George Brunis, Elmer Schoebel and a drummer, before they went to the Friars Inn.
281.q: Well, one of the first jobs I had was with Georgie Brunus, Elmer Schauble, and Ralph Snyder, I think the drummer. The drummer. The rest I can't...

139.t: First music jobs: speakeasy with the Hickman Brothers
139.s: His first paid gig was a speakeasy job for 60 cents with the Hickman Brothers and others, then work out on the Lakefront with Kid Clayton.
139.q: No tips, no, no tips. 60 cents what you made. Oh, for the long? Hot dog man was on the outside waiting for you to buy hot dogs. Out there. Out there.

284.t: First job playing guitar on Halloween
284.s: Married and playing at home, he is hired on a deposit dollar to play with an unnamed bass player's band.
284.q: Well, I was living right, at that time I was living right here on St. Philo Street between Roman and Prayer. That's right.

5.t: First paid jobs and summers with the brass band
5.s: Winstead and the brass band paid him the same as everyone; summers were fairs, with marches, overtures and popular tunes.
5.q: Well, now I can't remember the first job. But I think my first job was with this fellow I was telling you about. Winstead and he paid. I got paid. I can't remember what it was. But... And that's one thing about those fellows. That's where they all... Anytime I would work with this fellow Winstead…

127.t: First paid job in the country
127.s: His first paid job in Raceland at fifty cents; Paul Rose started him; his birthday is clarified.
127.q: Was in the country. Was in the country, right where I lived at. I was on a lawn. We got fifty cents a piece. And I got seventy-five cents. But the rest of them was, you know, fifty cents a piece. Plenty of money, too.

855.t: Playing at youth events, amateur festivals and New Orleans circles in Berlin
855.s: Playing for Jenike at the youth house and big festivals; forming circles around New Orleans jazz with named Berlin musicians.
855.ch: Discovering jazz and playing in Berlin
855.q: Yes, I didn't know what the events were, but then also the great events. The Sporthall and the great events were there, where thousands of people were there.

54.t: Bud's band grows to 18; first dance and Bud's big voice
54.s: The band grew with new horn players, played country clubs and parties, got its first dance from Mrs. Poole, and Bud's huge singing voice carried over the river.
54.q: And from then, well, he had chased away from home for a while and came back and met lots of musicians, different places, and he looked over the billboard and we would get in. Next was a trombone and there's a trumpet player. And on and, you know, like that, till the band got to about 18 strong. And…

884.t: Penny parties, field bands and a six-piece orchestra
884.s: They played penny parties; later a three-piece field band (piccolo, bass drum, snare) and then a six-piece orchestra with trumpet, bass, clarinet and guitar.
884.q: Oh, yeah. Yeah, the marches. Yeah, the marches. Yeah, the piccolo and a bass drum and a snare drum. Yeah. Just like the Army, you know, something like that. Yeah. Like the vipen drum bars. Yeah, that's it. And we used to play at parties like that. We used to play street, too. Used to call what you…

831.t: Joe Ellibush's band and lawn party jobs on bass horn
831.s: With Joe Ellibush, a poor trombonist who led the band, he played bass horn at lawn parties without piano.
831.q: Oh yeah, sure we had piano with us. Sure. And I remember when I played with, uh, Joe Ellibush's band. We never had no piano at that time. We used to play lawn parties. And they never had no pianos at the lawn parties. So you used to have to use the guitar or banjo.

138.t: Dating the exposition and Laine's birth year
138.s: Russell and Laine work out that Laine was about eleven at the exposition; his first paid job was a political rally at five dollars a piece.
138.q: 84, I believe. Now, I... You were born when? 75. 21st day of September. On the 21st day of September in 1873. So you'd be about 11 years old.

197.t: First paid job and spot jobs
197.s: First job on banjo with a piano player at a private party; spot work with Kazimer and Clayton.
197.q: No, we didn't have any regular jobs, just spotting around, that's all. I spotting around with Clayton too.

782.t: His first bands, with his brother and the Snakes
782.s: He first played irregularly with his brother, then a year with a modern Dixieland band.
782.q: Oh, that was another band. First I played with my brother. But that was just very irregular. No, just now and then I mean. Did the band have a name? No, I guess they had a name. When I came in my brother almost quit playing already. So he just played a few jobs that came up with friends, more…

909.t: First paid job for Senator Brady
909.s: His first jobs were Saturday-night dates for Brady, who paid Professor Humphrey's teaching.
909.q: I don't know The first job Because we used to have to play for Senator Brady Every Saturday night Yeah Then he used to throw up sacks of money You know And he'd have that there This for his people out there Well we had to go pray for him every Saturday night Because he was paying all the teaching…

967.t: Starting to sing with Huey Smith's group at the Moonlight Inn
967.s: Looking for work, King joined pianist Huey Smith and a drummer as singer, then was told he also needed to play guitar.
967.q: instrument? Well, my playing and performing was kind of a coincidence, you know, like I was looking for work one time and I couldn't find anything to do. So I started listening around and listening to groups of people like Huey Smith, which later became Huey Smith and Clowns, which was a pianist…

858.t: First New Orleans band: a seven-piece jazz band working nightly
858.s: He describes the first band, a seven-piece jazz band that worked every night for several months.
858.q: We had a seven-piece jazz band. It was very good. At one time we were working every night. That's what I did for about four or six months. Every night of the week we were working. Different places every night? Different places every night.

300.t: First jobs and the family band
300.s: Humphrey recalls his first job with guitarist Dan's lake-camp band and concerts with his grandfather.
300.q: Well, the first jobs I played, I played with a fellow named Dan. He was a guitar player. And he used to have a four-piece band, go out on the lake on Sundays. That was most of his work. Every Sunday he'd have a departure train that was lit up at little, uh, uh, places out there that was dancing.…

198.t: First band: the Ambrose Power job down the river
198.s: Barnes's first real job was a four-piece band with Ambrose, Henry Ford and others, playing all night at a dance down the river.
198.q: I'm reading, reading, reading. The first band I played in. I just remember it was, I believe it was Ambrose Power. Ambrose Power. Yeah. Lawrence took his uncle. I played, I played then with them down at Del Cron.

715.t: Day jobs, marriage and leaving St. Louis for Seattle
715.s: Before leaving in 1920 he worked in a foundry and packing house, played nightclubs a few nights a week, then took a $50 a week job on the coast.
715.q: No, not until I left St. Louis. During those years, before I left St. Louis, I would do some work. I married young, so I had to work. I didn't labor and work, packing house.
