756.t: First paid gigs at 13 and Jaski's double-booking
756.s: He started playing gigs very young, earned $20 the first time, and played with older musicians. Jaski would send him out with an amp and then show up partway through the night.
756.q: It just happened. I started playing very young, gigs. By the time I was 13 I was out on the weekends making money and, you know, and that was it. Once I got money in my pocket I was good to go.

442.t: First gigs and what they paid
442.s: His first gig with an accordionist paid ten dollars, then a Knights of Columbus dance paid 25; he decides on music.
442.q: And yeah that was it. I knew right then and there. It was 1958. I had started playing drums in school and I said that’s it, that’s it for me. And then actually what really was the kind of final decision-maker was I got my first gig, right? And the gig paid ten dollars, right? And I tell this story…

348.t: Deciding on music and the dime-a-dance job at $15 a week
348.s: Encouraged by praise, he stuck with music; his first dime-a-dance hall job paid $15 a week for late hours.
348.q: That was it. Especially when people tell you you play pretty good, so I figured none of the other kids could do that, I figured I’d better stay with this, if they think I can do it, well that’s what I did.

554.t: Catskills bebop band and early work at 17
554.s: He left a short Blue Cross job for music, playing resort hotel shows in the Catskills.
554.q: It seems like it became my career — I guess there were opportunities, whatever it was, when I was about 17. I had a little bebop band in the Catskill mountains, New York, and we were playing [scats] that type thing. So I grew up with that and I think just when I got out of high school I think just…

161.t: Practicing with his sister, high school band, first paid gig
161.s: His sister's teasing spurred practice; he played in high school band and mentions his first paid gig in Trenton.
161.ch: New York, the clarinet and first gigs
161.q: Oh, oh, oh. Well this is very deep. So anyhow, well let me finish the story about my sister. So I went home with the clarinet and I started to practice and she laughed and said “you sound like a duck,” which led me to practice. And I evidently improved very quickly. I mean I just ate it up. So then…

464.t: First paid job with Slide Hampton, $350 for one concert
464.s: Two weeks after quitting he plays a North Carolina concert with Slide Hampton's band for $350. He had refused other jobs while preparing, and has never worked outside music since.
464.q: Yeah. But it was me and Richard Williams, that was the trumpet section, and Slide Hampton and Garnett Brown was in the trombone section. Let’s see. Hubert Laws was playing tenor saxophone. And I can’t remember who else was in the band. But I mean it was a great band. And Slide was very popular.…

732.s: Pallo's first professional job at about fourteen, in a four-piece group with accordion, trumpet and drums, paid seven or fourteen dollars; he needed working papers.
732.q: Yes. Wow. I think first of all the union scale was seven dollars. I think it was seven or fourteen, something like that.

162.t: First paid job: replacing the trumpeter at Sylvan Beach
162.s: He filled in for a black band's trumpeter at Sylvan Beach, faking tunes from his repertoire.
162.q: Well I was playing in Sylvan Beach and there was a colored band there and the wife of the trumpet player chased him right into Oneida Lake.

684.t: First modern jazz group, jazz camp and first paid gigs
684.s: At 17 she meets players at a jazz camp, forms a band in Newcastle, then goes to the Sydney Conservatorium; early pay.
684.q: Yeah. I met some musicians — I was 17 at the jazz camp. I went to a classical camp, found out about a jazz camp, so the next school holiday I went to that jazz camp. And that’s where the first proper like modern jazz group that me and Andrew Dickenson who is a drummer who teaches at Sydney…

1004.t: Introduction; surviving the music business, clubs and Associated demos
1004.s: Phillips says she survived by playing piano and singing, working clubs opposite Bobby Short and then demos at Associated alongside young songwriters.
1004.q: Well let’s see — I know too many people who haven’t survived. I was very fortunate because I played piano. I could play piano and sing. And so when I came to New York I didn’t have to wait tables. I’ve done nothing in my life but music. And then the music business began, which is first playing in…

790.t: First paid gig and supportive parents
790.s: Playing pops concerts with symphonies, then his first pay of about $70 with high school band director; parents chaperoned underage gigs. Born 1970.
790.q: I think the first time I actually made money, I think it probably had to be about ninth grade I think. I had already been doing some classical performances, like orchestras and stuff, and my junior high school orchestra teacher had even gotten some of her students who excelled to perform, to do…

596.t: First professional job with King Kolax
596.s: Powell joined King Kolax's band in Port Arthur, Texas at about 16 while in college; being paid made him a professional in 1944.
596.q: Yeah. He was with Billy Eckstine’s band the same time as all the guys — I think Charlie Parker was there. In 1946 I think he broke off and organized his own band. And when I joined him he had a territory band, well not a territory, it was in Port Arthur, Texas, and there was this guy from my…

930.t: Subbing lead trumpet at the Fairmont Hotel show at 16
930.s: Contractor Jack Fisher hired the 16-year-old for a show and dance, and he played lead when the regular player arrived late.
930.q: so I get the experience to say that I’ve played a show so I can get other jobs to play shows and dances.” And it’s silence. And Jack Fisher says, “Be there at 7:00.” So now I show up there, right? And I get there early and we’re in the room and there’s like twelve musicians and typical talk-over.…

216.t: Picking up saxophone at 16 and first gigs
216.s: He kept clarinet and sax separate, played his first gig on New Year's Eve five weeks after starting sax, and later drove far for $15 gigs.
216.ch: Denver youth and University of Denver
216.q: Yeah I was one of those guys, yeah. I started out on clarinet and I always sort of kept the two tracks separate, you know I played clarinet and did all the legit stuff, the classical stuff, and at age 16 I picked up the saxophone and I remember five weeks later I played my first gig, it was New…

699.t: Teen band with Freddie Hubbard and James Spaulding; first road gig
699.s: Their teenage band played six nights a week at a club, with Al Plank on piano; he took a first road gig at sixteen with the Jazz Contemporaries.
699.q: Well I was fortunate in that Freddie Hubbard and James Spaulding and a lot of us, we had our own little bands and we were playing jazz. In fact we had a hot little band. My uncle was friendly with some gentlemen who owned a club in Indianapolis. And we had a gig, we worked six nights a week with…

356.t: Working with Gene Brant's band at age 12
356.s: Wartime opportunity: joined the union and played society band jobs, learned to read, and was paid like an adult.
356.q: Yeah it was great for me, yeah. I was young and I got in a union, I went down with a pipe. Gene Brant got me, and this was a great guy, a trombone player, and he worked at the George Washington Hotel, sort of a society band I guess, I really don’t remember now what it was we played. Although I…

487.t: First Latin band in the Catskills and the Latin hotel scene
487.s: Summers of 1958 and 1959 in the Catskills, a small Latin quartet playing pared-down Tito Puente arrangements, and why Latin bands played Jewish resort hotels.
487.ch: Growing up and discovering Latin music
487.q: Yes. A very small Latin band. It was just timbales, piano, bass, and trumpet. No conga, no other Latin percussion. And as a matter of fact the timbale player, every one of the timbale players were influenced by Tito Puente. And I heard the timbale player play some of these licks that to me were…

357.t: Forming the Catatonic Five, bourbon pay and the pizza story
357.s: Having heard the Fallacious Five jam, he formed his own band with Emerson Brown, Derry Hall and others, paid in bourbon; a Deke House gig ends with a pizza and Emerson's anchovy remark.
357.q: Silliman Hall. And the band at that time was Bob Krompart on cornet, Collier on trombone, John Fell was the clarinetist, the pianist was Pete Zeeveld, and Mike Beldock, who had a distinguished career as an attorney and still does, was the drummer in the band. And anyway I used to just sit there…

163.t: First gigs at 16 and Jimmy Walsh's band at Casino Gardens
163.s: He joined the union, worked weekends and singer jobs, then played with Jimmy Walsh and arranged for Jan Savitt.
163.q: Well I moved to Los Angeles, I was 16, so I joined the union there. And I was still going to school, I would work weekends, club dates they would call them. It wasn’t — I mean not a lot of guys want to take a chance on a 16-year-old, but my dad knew, people knew him and so he contacted people, and…

512.t: First paying gig and the Metronome All-Stars
512.s: First paid gigs were rhythm and blues and top 40s with a group called The Metronome All-Stars.
512.q: You know we was doing all that kind of stuff. So you know we had a group, I guess it was called The Metronome All-Stars. So we’d be doing top 40s —

575.t: Compton Community Center dance, tunes, and time versus perfect notes
575.s: The first gig was a dance playing standards and blues with Big Jay McNeely around. Smith argues that good time matters more than correct notes and that he is now a moldy fig wanting swing.
575.q: Well we were playing things like “Moonlight in Vermont,” “Blue Moon,” and there was a saxophone player out here, Big Jay McNeely.

488.t: First paying gig at the Elks Club with Pat Patrick
488.s: His father hired him on drums at fourteen, alongside baritone saxophonist Pat Patrick.
488.q: Yeah. Working with my father in the Elks Club. Because the Elks Club would have regular Friday night or Saturday night affair and my father broke me in as the drummer when I was fourteen years old. And as a matter of fact he hired a young baritone saxophone player who turned out to be my age and…

943.t: Sitting in at fifteen and taking Dave Berry's gig
943.s: His father makes him sit in on a Sunday session, Jimmy Ford approves, and Dave Berry hands him the gig.
943.q: Well what happened was the drummer who had the gig at this particular club that had Sunday afternoon sessions, was a fellow named Dave Berry, who unfortunately has left us, a very sweet man. Hell of a drummer. And it was Dave’s gig and he’d come over to my house a couple of times just to show me…

933.t: A cover band and a one-album Mercury deal
933.s: They played James Brown and Otis Redding covers; as Giant he later made one album for Mercury.
933.q: Well the thing was, it’s funny you said that. We were sort of a cover band. We didn’t really write a lot of originals. We were covering a lot of stuff: James Brown, Otis Redding, you know we played some Joe Tex. We were doing a lot of covers. So I don’t think we really dreamed too much about having…

1005.t: Kinds of gigs in Milan as a teenager
1005.s: Milan gigs ranged from jazz clubs to weddings, and he learned to make sure hirers knew the band played jazz.
1005.q: Yeah it’s the usual combination that applies to this very day. Sometimes it’s a concert in a jazz club. Sometimes it’s a jazz concert in a theater. Sometimes it was a jazz festival. Sometimes it was just a restaurant gig, background. Sometimes it was a wedding. Now the trouble back then happened…

845.t: First tuba gig at Your Father's Moustache
845.s: His first tuba gig was at Your Father's Moustache in Philadelphia, followed by a summer at the Summer's Point club.
845.q: Um hum. My first gig out of college. This was one of the things that started making me like the instrument. My first gig was on — not really first gig, my first gig on tuba was at a place called Your Father’s Moustache. There was a whole chain of these things in Philadelphia and New York, St.…

936.t: Playing trumpet in church, Easter solos and weddings
936.s: The minister asked him to play classical trumpet solos, which led to weddings and receptions; he says church is a forgiving place to start performing.
936.q: Well the trumpet was there the whole time and I always listened to the trumpet, but in terms of you know you have more opportunities to sing in church than you do to play but actually what would happen is we had a great minister, Reverend Brown, and he loved classical music. And he started asking…

446.t: Playing a club at 15 to support the family
446.s: After his father's death Tiberi worked in a club at 15 earning 30 dollars a week, and joined Bob Chester's orchestra in 1948.
446.q: Well at 15 — my father died after an accident actually — when I was 12, and at 15 I was in a club. And ironically I was singing “Caledonia” and playing the “Woodchopper’s Ball” you know with a small group with a trumpet and sax. And I was making 30 dollars a week and that was supporting the family.…

363.t: Records, Kid Ory and the Apex Stompers
363.s: He wanted to play traditional jazz like Kid Ory, bought 78s, and the band played for beer until its London billing coincided with his call-up.
363.ch: Discovering jazz and the trad band
363.q: bowled over by this. Strictly traditional jazz. I wanted to play traditional jazz. By that time I knew who Kid Ory was and I was aware that that was the kind of jazz music I wanted to have a go at. And we all felt the same, you know, quite purist and just wanted to have a go at it.

364.s: Wedding jobs at twelve to fifteen dollars a night with small groups, as a proving ground.
364.q: Trumpet, a tenor player, usually clarinet, tenor, maybe no bass. Guitar probably, drums and piano. Small groups. And we played the typical wedding songs and the “Miami Beach Rumba.”

122.t: First paid gigs: Pat Patterson, the Drum Club and Rose Murphy
122.s: His first money came from after-hours piano-drum jobs and subbing for Saunders King's drummer; Rose Murphy stole tips.
122.q: Oh yeah. Let’s see. I guess it was with Patterson. Pat Patterson played the piano. And he was a good piano player, schooled in theory and harmony. And Pat used to get gigs at these after hour places so we worked at a place called Minnie’s Can Do, up on Fillmore Street in the Western Addition, after…

983.t: Playing gigs with his father and Philadelphia cabarets
983.s: He describes club dates, dances and parties with his father, jazz being accessible then, and the Seven Eleven ballroom cabarets with Jimmy Heath.
983.ch: Growing up with his father's music
983.q: Um hum. Yeah. But you know jazz in those days I mean it was accessible to everybody and everybody loved it. I mean it wasn’t pigeon-holed. I mean we used to play [sings] “Straighten up and fly right — Straighten up and fly right — Straighten up and fly right

740.t: First gigs and dances in the fifties
740.s: He cannot pinpoint his first professional job; he played neighborhood dances, where good time mattered, with Lindy, mambo and calypso crowds.
740.q: A gig? Gee I can’t, it’s hard to really pinpoint my first professional job although I know I played, I had a set of drums and I was playing and people would call, they knew I could play drums, so they would call around, you know the different people in the neighborhood that had dances or something…

552.s: His parents took him seriously only at eighteen; he played garage, R&B and disco bands for money.
552.q: Yeah. Actually they were. I think not until I was eighteen did they really begin to take me seriously as someone who wanted to do this professionally. I think, as any parent, you think okay well they’re going to go through several phases. But no, even as a teenager I was playing in garage bands and…

85.t: First gigs: Rex Stewart's matinee and Willy the Lion Smith's trio
85.s: He gets a dollar-and-a-quarter matinee on Rex Stewart's recommendation, then joins Willie the Lion Smith's trio and is told to get an alto, which his parents buy.
85.q: Well, I was about fourteen, and, oh, I think after I had the instrument a number of months, I had one gig, an afternoon gig that Rex Stewart took me on, too, because they were lacking . . . something had happened to their saxophonist. It was a matinee at a club on 135th Street. He said if I could…

703.t: Garage jam sessions and the Pandora's Box coffeehouse band
703.s: After the fiasco he and Herbie formed a group with Nat Brown and a conga player, held jam sessions at his parents' garage and worked Pandora's Box on the Sunset Strip.
703.ch: Pasadena jam sessions, Billy Mitchell and Mingus
703.q: I realized either two things: I was either going to lay there on the floor, from getting decked like that, from that Sunday punch, and have everybody at school say, “See, I told you,” or I was going to get up off the canvas and make my mother proud. So me and Herbie, we started hanging out with…

503.t: After high school: a popular local band and the Club Sudan
503.s: He worked constantly with his own band, his mother pushed college, and he began meeting visiting stars at Club Sudan jam sessions.
503.ch: High school, Dizzy and Wayne State
503.q: I decided that I was, and I was doing well after I graduated from high school. I mean, I had, I was working all the time and practicing hard and getting better and better, and had a little band, probably the most, one of the most popular bands in town at that time. Local jazz polls I would win. And…

101.t: Sy McField and Dollar Bill and his Small Change
101.s: Terry played with an old pianist in a small St. Louis band, where older players hired kids cheaply.
101.q: Dollar Bill. Hah-hah. That was a little – a small band that I worked with in St. Louis when we were all at the stage where we were just getting involved and were able to gig because we knew the tunes, and we were seeking the experience of the old pros. So he was one of the old pros. I guess it was…

116.t: The Groovy Boys and first paid dances
116.s: He forms a teenage R&B band with Roger Dickerson and earns his first money at school dances.
116.q: Yeah. I started to play some jobs, primarily on tenor saxophone. We started this band, youngsters in high school. We called it the Groovy Boys. Boy, you think that ain’t corny!

527.t: The teen band, Lunceford's advice and the band's pay
527.s: The band stayed in Arizona; Lunceford gave them his booking agent's address; the trombonist managed the band and they made about $5 a night.
527.q: Well, yes. We would stay in the state of Arizona and go around to other towns and play a dance here and there, like the Elks or something like that, but we didn’t leave the state of Arizona. We were like 14, 15, 16 [years old]. There were a couple of guys who were older than us, but they had day…

224.t: Parents' reaction, $12 a week and early jazz gigs
224.s: He kept going to school half asleep, brought money home, and played straight-ahead jazz in nightclubs.
224.q: I didn’t stop school immediately. I was still going to school, but sleeping in school. I couldn’t concentrate. But I would accomplish a lot financially, and I was trying

135.t: Playing the Ritz Bar in Wilmington, Delaware, and meeting Clifford Brown
135.s: Heath recalls commuting to Wilmington with the Hollis Hoppers, the segregation there, and a shy young Clifford Brown saying he would play jazz too.
135.q: Uh, I don’t know if that was there then. We used to commute from Philly, but I’m not sure if we used to stay down there. It was a little segregated down there at that time even.

471.t: Cheap early gigs with Benny Golson and Carrington Visor
471.s: Cobb describes unpaid gigs around town with Benny Golson, a Lady Day-style singer, and tenor Carrington Visor.
471.ch: Growing up and learning drums in Washington
471.q: Tenor player. Sounded like Gene Ammons. Had that big sound. You say, “Where’s it coming from?” Just a little guy like that. It was him – it would be him and Benny Golson. At that time, Benny Golson was playing like Dexter Gordon. So they would get on the stand, and they would go through that thing…

225.t: Musical friends and LaVon Kemp's band
225.s: Schoolmates such as Eldridge Morrison, Erroll Grandy and Bill Stafford, who played social dances in LaVon Kemp's and later Jimmy Coe's bands.
225.q: Oh, yes. There was Eldridge Morrison. There was Vincent Stewart. None of them ever stayed with the music situation other than myself. Erroll Grandy, of course. There was a trumpet player whose name was Merrill Laswell. There was a fella whose

165.t: Professional at eleven on WSPD radio with the Swing Buddies
165.s: He earned $125 a week at eleven singing on WSPD Toledo with a vocal quartet that protected him.
165.q: I was with another group of guys. We were called the Swing Buddies. It was four guys – three men and me – because I was really a kid. They used to take care of me

111.t: Art Martigan and the Crystal Lounge: first job with Wardell Gray
111.s: Going to Detroit he met drummer Art Martigan, who handed him the six-night Crystal Lounge job with Wardell Gray.
111.q: Oh no, not yet. I started later on I guess. I started to go to Detroit. Cause there was nothing in Pontiac. Just a lot of drinking! I went to Detroit and I met Art Martigan and Art Martigan was playing with Wardell Gray and he – I’d go back to that club and listen to him. And he played so smoothly.…

576.t: Mingus pushes her to sing in a Toledo club
576.s: Visiting her half-sister in Toledo, she is called up by Mingus with Lee Konitz and sings Yesterdays in her first club bass-and-voice performance.
576.q: Her name was Donna. Donna Dawson. And she‟s, she‟s quite the lady, you know. I really got to really know her a little better now, my later years. But uh, I said, “Mingus, Charles Mingus is playing in this club, and I‟d like to go hear him.” So she said yes. So we went. And it was Charles Mingus. I…

505.t: Club dates in the Catskills as his training ground
505.s: Booked in the Catskills from age 13, he played club dates in a tuxedo; the mix of styles trained him and he had the Impromptu Quartet.
505.q: The three-part harmony written out. This family – this mother, Fay, who just died – amazing. I was in touch with her all the way through – she booked you in the Catskills as soon as you could play. I was there. I’m 13 years old. My first summer – because I’m September. So right July, August of my…

555.t: Meeting Minnie Hightower, Vi Redd and Alice Young
555.s: At school she met Minnie Hightower and joined the group, practicing at the Ross Snyder playground with Vi Redd and Alice Young, the only close girls.
555.ch: Los Angeles youth and Miss Hightower
555.q: [cannot recall.] I met her, and she was thrilled with my playing the trombone and all that. We had a good thing going for many years. We played everywhere. We practiced at the Ross Snyder playground. [At night in the summertime they played in the parks.]

228.t: Cocktail-sip dances inherited from Sonny Rollins
228.s: Rollins controlled the fraternity-dance jobs paying eight to twelve dollars; when he went away he passed them to McLean; Rollins returned transformed and joined Miles first.
228.ch: Heroin and the Miles Davis years
228.q: $10, $9, or $12. In that range. $8. It depends. Sonny used to have control of that, Sonny Rollins. Sonny was – I must say now that Sonny was an important part of my learning experience right during this particular time, because I looked up to Sonny.

400.t: First bass jobs: Huey Swift, Johnny Long, $3 gigs and pianist Stump King
400.s: Hinton plays club dates with Johnny Long's band, lending money to Eddie South between jobs, and notes that well-connected players like Stump King got the work.
400.ch: Capone's Chicago, the union and hired by Cab
400.q: Yeah. This Johnny Long is a trumpet player. Not a good trumpet player but a very wise guy. He had the club dates scene covered like Mitch Roberts. His name is Johnny Long and he wasn‟t a good trumpet player but he was wise enough to get good guys all the time. Joe Williams was the vocalist [laugh].…

426.t: Visiting studios and working at Nola Studio in New York
426.s: After high school he visited studios, saw their machines, and had his first job at Nola.
426.q: No this was after high school, just. There was a place in New York City called Nola Studio, and I used to see the machines they had. And I actually worked there, that was my first job, I have my social security card to prove it. It’s got Nola’s name on it to prove it. So I worked there for a while…

123.t: The Downbeat Club and meeting Serge Chaloff
123.s: Underage, he gets into Philadelphia's Downbeat Club with Serge Chaloff and hears local musicians such as Specs Wright and Jimmy Heath.
123.q: ... who was a complete nut. And he took me up there, I was underage but he took me up there. They had Specs Wright on drums, Jimmy Golden, pianist, and Jimmy Oliver, tenor saxophonist. Of course Jimmy Heath was up there a lot, and all kinds of great musicians. Red Rodney, so I met a lot of those…

63.t: Cleveland bands and high pay in Prohibition years
63.s: Aaronson was his first name band, but before that he played in Cleveland bands chasing good books and earned $175+ a week as a teenager.
63.ch: Early years: Cleveland, Aaronson, New York
63.q: Irving Aaronson was the first so-called “name band,” national band. Up ’til then I played with much better bands. They weren’t good, but some guys around Cleveland had a pretty good band. I would go wherever the band was good, wherever the book [“book”: in jazz parlance, the collection of musical…

509.t: The teddy bear and her first singing, and pay of $175
509.s: She sang Melancholy Baby for a man's gift of a bear, was paid $175, until her parents stopped it.
509.q: Okay. This was a dining room that I was, you know, sneaked my age. At that time you had to be eighteen to play in where they served alcohol. Okay. Well, I changed my age, and this old man would come in. He was so fine. He was good looking, debonair, you know. He came every evening and had dinner,…

528.t: First gigs and Cal Massey's band
528.s: At about sixteen he played house parties; his sister-in-law Khadijah sang in trumpeter Cal Massey's band, called 'Folks'.
528.q: Yeah, well I started when I was sixteen, so I’d say about . . . I’m trying to figure out . . . I’d say around sixteen or something like that and that’s when I got gigs playing house parties sometimes you know . . . they heard about the band. We had a guy we called him Billy and he heard about our…

137.t: Family gigs and the drummer who was a Negro League ballplayer
137.s: The family got wedding and dance jobs through school, with an older drummer who played baseball for a Kansas City Monarchs-type team as contractor.
137.q: Yeah, and he played with the Pittsburgh -- you know, they had a lot of teams around, I forget the name of them now, Kansas City Monarchs, -- that was Satchel Paige's team.

80.t: First dance job in Brewton and the man with the pistol
80.s: He talks his religious mother into letting him play a dance in Brewton, sees trap drums for the first time, and a gunman scares the one-eyed clarinetist.
80.ch: Boyhood in Evergreen and Calhoun school
80.q: No. Ma Rainey, that's different, but I knew Ma Rainey, played for her. Sure. Knew Ma Rainey. And the minstrel -- you asked me the first job, they gave a dance in Brewton, Alabama, that was about 20 miles from Evergreen. And they were short of a man. They needed somebody to be the trumpet player,…

377.t: Making the rounds of Kansas City clubs for a piano job
377.s: Basie describes looking for work in Kansas City, where clubs had tiny combinations and a piano spot was easy to find.
377.ch: Early career: vaudeville and Kansas City
377.q: No, just the way's how you do a thing, how you do a thing. I'll (inaudible) little tricky ways. I mean, not tricky, but what you did do, when you go around and see where you can go, see where you could get in, sneak in and whatever happen's, whatever --

614.t: House band at the Eagles Ballroom in Milwaukee
614.s: In high school he played tenor and clarinet in the ballroom house band five nights a week, meeting visiting bands like Paul Whiteman's.
614.q: : Later, but by that time I was in high school and I was now in the house band at the Eagles Ballroom. And we had many bands coming in across the country to play opposite, including Paul Whiteman. So I got to meet a lot of these people whom I had been hearing only on records and on the radio, and…

145.t: First saxophone jobs and falling asleep in Spanish class
145.s: The market-opening band led to many jobs, taking over his father's engagements, until parents curbed his working because school suffered.
145.q: I was in high school. I was about 14, 15 years old. I was about 15. So, I went out that Saturday and I played on the job and it went over. So, the next week, there was an opening of another market and the man called and asked for the same band that played for his opening of his market. So I went to…

17.t: Botching the Charlie Skeets audition; fired by Sylvester Lewis
17.s: Two more failures: nerves ruin an audition for Charlie Skeets and poor time costs him a dancing-school job; he resolves to study harder.
17.q: Yeah, that was after Jelly Roll. Then I did another little thing, up around the same Band Box and Rhythm Club, it was a great arranger around there and he used to do a lot of dancing school gigs. Name was Charlie Skeets.

4.t: Getting bookings by word of mouth
4.s: Small Arizona towns spread news of the piano-and-drums duo quickly, and drunk German patrons paid in advance.
4.ch: Second session: boyhood, brothers and early road years
4.q: Well, he had played around there, and people knew he was a piano player but they didn't know he had drums, but after ...after one or two dances, why then everybody in town knew it, you know. Them little towns--everybody in town knew it.

106.t: Hired from a cab: forming a five-piece band
106.s: A man in a hackney cab, shouting 'musician', wanted an orchestra; Briggs took him to the Flea Pits and formed a five-piece with Salnave, a drummer, a pianist and a guitarist.
106.q: So, I said, 'Okay,' and I went to work with him, and I stayed with him, and one of the days, just a few days after, while I was going to one of his rehearsals 'cause he made arrangements, you know.

89.t: First job with the Douglas Debating Society sextet
89.s: The six-piece club band played one dance at Oddfellow's Hall for a dollar and a half each, and the club voted to take the money back.
89.q: Well, I would like to give you a little story about our first job that I played. You know, we organized a band in Springfield and there were six of us. And we were all members of a club called the Douglas Debating Society and we had rehearsed until we got so we could play about four tunes.

0.t: Playing jazz gigs in East Chicago, Indiana
0.s: His first work was a small group playing night gigs and holidays in East Chicago, riding the Illinois Central and passing the hat.
0.ch: National Guard band and first jobs in Chicago
0.q: I'd worked with -- well, this little group out -- just out of Chicago called Indiana, which is still part of the city of Chicago, but East Chicago, and that is going into like East Chicago. 380.t: Banjo Bernie and his first paid gigs in Atlantic City and Philadelphia
380.s: He describes a bandleader who rarely paid, a Philadelphia nightclub gig in the Prohibition era, and counts it his first professional work.
380.ch: Youth, the road and arrival in California
380.q: Then... Let's see, I left out a period in Atlantic City when I was still going to school. I ran into a guy... There's always a guy like this in every young musician's life, I guess, who gets the young musicians and doesn't pay them. Banjo Bernie was such a guy. And I used to gig with his band, and…

758.s: Playing basketball games and house parties in Homestead, staying out late and picking up money.

232.t: First gigs in Tulsa with William Ball and T.D. Thomas
232.s: He picks up gigs with William Ball and pianist T.D. Thomas, and during a trouble call hears a high school group in the Royal Annex Hall.
232.ch: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
232.q: I began to get around and meet some of the musicians in Tulsa, so I got acquainted with a young man who was working for an oil company, William Ball, and he said he would call me up when he got a gig. I made a few gigs with him and another man I got acquainted with, T.D. Thomas, a piano player, and…

91.t: First paid job at Connors Inn with Bubber Miley
91.s: Bubber Miley took him along to a gig on 135th Street paying $1.25, his first paid job, after sitting in around Harlem.
91.q: Yes, some. Yes, right. I started getting some jobs around, the first of which I remember for which I was paid. Of course, I used to go around and sit in, as we did in those days.

383.t: Talladega College, then Detroit and the first club dates
383.s: After one year of music major at Talladega, Wilson went to Detroit in summer 1929, joined Local 5 and worked club dates with Howard Bunch and Everett Barksdale.
383.q: That would have been in Detroit late in the year, 1929. I went to college one year in Talladega, took a music major there under a very talented man named Tergee Debolis (phonetic) -- an excellent classical pianist and a master of harmony, and really knew how to teach the students the basic things…

18.t: Playing around Atlanta in the Hamilton and Montgomery band
18.s: He worked a good deal while at school, in the Hamilton and Montgomery band.
18.q: Oh, I did quite a bit of work while I was there. Yeah, I was in school and we had a band there. Merrill Mayer Hamilton and they called it the Hamilton and Montgomery band.

92.t: Playing in his mother's band as a boy
92.s: From about age twelve he played in his mother's band alongside pros like Lorenzo Wardell and Alton Moore, and Handy's band would visit the house.
92.q: Well, that was from around 12, 13. I was playing, you know, with her band then. And she had let's see one guy I remember particularly, his name was Lorenzo Wardell. He had played with let's see -- was it McKinney's cotton pickers? From Detroit. Yeah, a very fine -- but any way, he played in our…

93.t: First onstage with Buck and Bubbles at Loew's State
93.s: Green, about seventeen, is paid by Buck and Bubbles and first goes onstage with them at Loew's State, with Nazarro making everything legal.
93.ch: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
93.q: Well, I was going on 17, you see. But by them being adults and through the business mind of Nat Nazarra, I mean everything was legal. We'd have the proper permission, you see.

566.t: Getting hired to sing at the Vendome and dressing from thrift shops
566.s: The hotel hired her to sing with the home-town musicians. Worried about having no clothes, she bought gowns at thrift shops and impressed Mrs. Clore with her wardrobe.
566.q: And so, you know, Mrs. Clore, Mr. Bill Clore and his wife, and she was very stately, you know. And I said, 'I ain't got no clothes to wear here'. And a friend of mine knew where they had some thrift shops and she said, Helen I'm going to take you to these thrift shops where the people, they buy all…

384.s: A 1950 Long Island Press article recounts his birth, high school band, first paid job on banjo with Weems, and sessions with the leading names of the twenties.
384.ch: N'goma drums and the scrapbook clippings

385.t: Leaving Newport News for Washington and the amateur shows
385.s: Three boys head to Washington on a truck, sing and play for a dollar a night, and do amateur shows; he changes his nickname from Teeny to Tiny.
385.q: I tell everybody I wasn't No'd, if you know what I mean. We left Newport News on a truck with about I'd say three or 4 dollars between the 3 of us. Just had enough heart & guts to go out & go to Washington. At that time you could get a meal for about 15¢. We

386.t: Learning from Trent and his first paid piano job in Athens, Texas
386.s: Trent lets him sit in on rehearsals and teaches him; he gets his first professional job in Athens, and is thrown out of a club after playing only one song.
386.ch: Learning piano, dancing and Alphonso Trent
386.q: Yeah, Alphonso was the piano player. He liked me and he used to...then I used to start bugging him to show me things. Whenever we would go...say if we were playing the Adolphus Hotel, we may arrive at the place an hour before, you understand, and he may be practicing like, learning a new song or…

148.t: First job at a Long Beach hotel
148.s: At fourteen or fifteen a neighbor saxophonist got him a summer job as pianist in a kid band, which his mother opposed and his father allowed.
148.q: It was the same job, and it was playing. I was about fourteen or fifteen and the family usually took a bungalow, or a house for the summer at Rockaway Beach, and I had a neighbor that lived across the street from me who was a saxophone player, and he came

95.t: Too young to sing in Chicago clubs
95.s: She was not singing in Chicago clubs because she was too young; she began after returning from Detroit and recalls getting in with a pianist friend.
95.q: I was too young, I was too young in those days, I didn't know how to do -- I didn't know (unintelligible). I was too young to go in them clubs (unintelligible). They wouldn't let me go in places. After it got to be (unintelligible), I knew a lot of people here. I knew a lot of girls here,…

168.t: Playing dances with Sonny Marshall and his Harlem Stompers
168.s: With a car from his father he traveled to Newark and Passaic to play adult dances in Sonny Marshall's small combo, his first experience in a jazz group.
168.q: No, there weren't any bands performing in Englewood. I find that, when I started playing the bass fiddle, I used to -- oh, let's see, I was about at least -- oh, 15, 16, or possibly 17, I'd say. I used to travel to other towns like Newark, and I joined a little jazz combo. And by that time I was…

387.t: French Line kids' band and Columbia Blue Lions
387.s: The kids' band plays French Line ships; at Columbia he joins the Blue Lions and studies liberal arts.

169.t: Oklahoma City: Henry Bridges' drive-in quartet and Bill Powell
169.s: Tenor player Henry Bridges lets him take up tips and teaches him songs; singer Bill Powell then takes him to Seminole.
169.q: But anyway, we did that for a while, and I got so I could eat by taking up the change, and the guys would chip in and give me something to have so I could go to a restaurant, after we got back in town, and eat, and so forth

31.t: Catching Rock and White's show numbers at Suntaug Lake Inn
31.s: At Suntaug Lake Inn he learns show songs by seeing every Boston opening, and earns $200 from performers who visit.
31.ch: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
31.q: : Yeah, Eddie Cantor, see, I used to play down on Suntaug Lake Inn, down in Lynnfield, Massachusetts about 17, nearly 20 miles outside of Boston.

81.t: First paid job and wanting to compose rather than play
81.s: He cannot say who first paid him; he never cared about money or being a pianist and wanted to write tunes.
81.ch: Reel 1: childhood, first songs, Fats Waller
81.q: Oh, that would be doggone just next to impossible for me to tell you who gave me my first pennies for playing because I never cared about playing for money, and I never cared about being a pianist, to tell you the truth.

413.t: First paying job in a bootleg dance place
413.s: At fifteen he played for dances in a Prohibition bootleg joint for $2 a night, had his first gin, and his father won the money back at cards.
413.q: Well, I started playing for dances in a place that was a bootleg place. This was during Prohibition and they sold drinks and they had lady entertainers there. There's another name for that kind of place, too.

238.t: Playing with Marshall Royal in San Pedro
238.s: In the late 1930s she played piano in a trio at a San Pedro club with Alton Red and saxophonist Marshall Royal.
238.q: Oh, that was in the -- that must have been in the '30s, the latter '30s, the latter part of the '30s. Before I started working with -- before I started recording or anything, naturally. But I can't --

7.t: Hired by Kid Carter's band in Minot, North Dakota
7.s: Overstreet in Topeka gets him a telegram offer; he travels to Minot to join Kid Carter's four-piece band playing one-night dances, including reels and square dances.
7.q: Yeah, that was a band in Topeka. So evidently... I often think about it. Evidently, when I went home that summer after I finished school... If I didn't give him my address, evidently he got it from the school. So he sent me a telegram that said he had a job for me out in Minot, North Dakota. I…

171.t: Deluxe Melody Boys and George Corley's Royal Aces
171.s: Cousins sang with the Deluxe Melody Boys, which became George Corley's Royal Aces, where Ramey started late 1931.
171.ch: Growing up with music in Austin
171.q: And at the same time they, my brothers and my cousins, they'd sing in quartets. And then this Ira Glasgow, he went on to sing in that Deluxe Melody Boys Band.

473.s: The boat needed a trumpet and clarinet; Jones refused to go without his buddy William Granger, so the leader took both trumpets.

112.s: When Freddy Tunstall walks out, Mr. Brown insists Wooding play upstairs at the Belmont cabaret and he struggles through the keys.
